By Samuel L. Leiter

June 2, 2025: Molière’s 1673 farce, The Imaginary Invalid, has had perhaps half a dozen professional New York revivals over the past century, most of short duration, and few of great historic interest. None of its three Broadway revivals, in 1917, 1922 (with Charles Coburn), and 1967, lasted more than eight performances. Of its handful of Off-Broadway showings, those by the Pearl Theatre Company in 2004 and Mabou Mines in 2012 appear to have been the most notable. I saw none, though, and also missed the recent Molière in the Park version. Each of this trio of revivals is said to have scored critical points in its approach. 

One can certainly see the possibilities in the disappointing revival now at New Work Stages, directed by Jesse Berger for his Red Bull Theater Company, which did far better in 2107 with The Government Inspector starring a brilliant Michael Urie. Jeffrey Hatcher, who prepared that script, is also responsible for the present adaptation, which, like Berger’s direction, puts its thumb on the farce scale, with enough scatological shtick to go through a Costco-size package of toilet paper at a single sitting. 

As is well known, The Imaginary Invalid (during a performance of which the playwright, in the leading role, died), is famous mainly for its satire of both hypochondria and the greedy, incompetent quacks who make a living off the fears of nosophobics. Molière’s play, like others in his canon, mingles criticism of a leading character’s extremism—for example, religion in Tartuffe, social climbing in The Bourgeois Gentleman, misanthropy in The Misanthrope, and the medical profession here and in The Doctor in Spite of Himself—with family conflict based on romantic attachments. Then, of course, there’s the soubrette, typically a saucy maid, like Toinette (Sarah Stiles) in The Imaginary Invalid, with an overall flavoring of standardized types and humor influenced by commedia dell’arte. Sometimes, as in this play, music and dance have a role, The Imaginary Invalid having been conceived as a comedy-ballet. 

So the Red Bull production has some songs, and even a bit of dance (choreography by Tracy Bersley), if not ballet, and its plot retains the traditional features. A rich, obstinate father, Argan (Mark Linn-Baker), has a beautiful daughter, Angelique (Emilie Kouatchou). She is in love with Cléante (John Yi), but dad wants her to marry instead a doofus doctor, Thomas Diafoirus (Russell Daniels). He’s the son of Argan’s physician, Dr. Diafoirus (Arnie Burton), which means he can have 24/7 service for his imagined ailments. There are also Argan’s gold-digging new wife, Béline (Emily Swallow) and her canny lawyer, De Bonnefoi (Manoel Felciano), who need to figure out the legal ways she—not Angelique—can obtain old Argan’s money when he dies. This allows for satire at the legal profession’s tricks. In Hatcher’s version we also get the suggestion of a romantic link between wife and lawyer that’s not in Molière’s play. 

Meanwhile, before the crafty Toinette crafts a solution to Angelique and Cléante’s dilemma, a whole lot of stage time is consumed with broad physical humor involving the hapless Argan and a stream of clownish doctors, with lots of running around through doors that never close but when they slam. Naturally, there are comically exaggerated props to facilitate Argan’s enemas. It’s the kind of farce that depends on a perfectly timed ensemble, with split-second business and innately funny actors who can make it seem both second nature and hilarious, the way first-rate productions of shows like The Play That Goes Wrong or Operation Mincemeat do. 

In the abstract, it’s possible to imagine a truly laugh-worthy production of The Imaginary Invalid, provided it involved a well-balanced company of farceurs under the direction of someone with a clever, insightful conception. It could go in several different directions, with its potential targets of hypochondria, medical overkill, pharmaceutical ethics, and so on, with a strong infusion of contemporary healthcare concerns used as markers of relevance. 

This production, however, not only lacks the ensemble it requires, it goes for the comic jugular while never getting past its anus. I was bewildered at the preview I attended by audience members laughing at nearly every line, while, for me, each such line only made the patient on the stage seem one step closer to flatlining. From the first words spoken, the actors seemed intent on showing, in case we didn’t get it, that they were in a sidesplitting play, and the pushing never stopped, even when—and it was more often than you might think—the pacing was more suitable for a play about someone with terminal cancer. I kept wondering why more music hadn’t been incorporated to help make things sprightlier, and perhaps also comment on the incidents.

Mark Linn-Baker’s Argan is, for all the silly things he’s put through, rather dully grounded and unflappable; he can be quite funny in the right material, but Molière eludes him. To be fair, I suspect even Nathan Lane would struggle to get laughs in this role. Others, like the usually reliable comedic actor, Arnie Burton, who mugs his way through several roles, or the cockily self-assured Sarah Stiles, appear to be forcing the humor. As Thomas, the wannabe suitor, Russell Daniels brings nearly Chris Farley proportions to the role, offering, in his deliberately childish costume, a sight gag chuckle on his first appearance; unfortunately, he needs more than heft to keep the yocks coming. For all the cast’s manic energy, the play never inspires deep laughter; those not on its wave length may sometimes feel an onset of the vapors. Fret not; its 80-minute runtime is a true restorative.

Beowulf Boritt has contributed a charmingly baroque unit set in the 17th-century mode, with doors at either side and a standing screen up center. Tilly Grimes’s costumes capture the period colorfully, Sun Ju Kim’s wigs amplify the period ambience, and Mextly Couzin does nicely with the lighting. But these features are little more than Botox on a lifeless patient—an elaborate façade that disguises the lack of vitality at the heart of the production. Beneath the visual flourish, the pulse of Molière’s satire struggles to beat, smothered by an uninspired operation that leaves the patient gasping for air.

The Imaginary Invalid ** 1/2

By Isa Goldberg

June 1, 2025: Among the worst nightmares is the one where you’re watching a play, and the conversation on stage feels so deadly, the atmosphere so stifling, and the proposed antagonist so pompous, it’s got to be a disaster. 

Watching Shellshocked, set on a cubby hole of a stage, in a small space at 59E59 Theaters, felt like the only thing to do to survive the full 70 minutes was to try and listen. Because if you don’t listen now, and there are only two actors on the stage, you’re going to get shot down when they reveal what this is really, all about. 

Well, it doesn’t take long before playwright Philip Stokes’ deadly two hander turns into a duel between an artist, and a savage madman. What unfolds is so completely surprising, that if you manage to get through those early introductions, what awaits is a horrific portrait of greed, hate, and envy. That is Lupine, a reputable portrait painter.

A dirty-looking, middle aged man, Lee Bainbridge’s Lupine is invidious from the get-go, questioning the young apprentice about the brand of a cardboard box he shows him; if it’s truly brown; if he’s a mama’s boy; if he polishes his own shoes; if he has a good metabolism. Then he persists at needling him about crying — when he cries, what makes him cry, when did he last cry – Wesley just stands stiffly, far too eager to please is he.

In that role, Jack Stoke’s vulnerable look reveals the shell-shocked soldier, returning from WWII, suffering from PTSD. Wearing an oversized suit that belonged to his recently deceased father, he looks painfully misplaced. But he’s there because Lupine, having seen his portfolio, and his drawings, has beckoned him to assist him in his studio. 

Lupine, the gamer, like the central character of Sleuth, uses every trick and tease he can to snare his victim. Ultimately trying to switch roles with Wesley, he turns him into the destroyer so that he can be the creator.  That, with a twisted confession about murdering his own father, leads Lupine to remark, “That souson of information has painted a very different picture. And that is what great art is my boy. Not the pictures we make but the pictures we create inside the mind.” What insidious thinking is that? And what a strategy for a portrait painter — to extinguishing life through terror.

With Lupine’s most absurd game, to force Wesley into painting his demise, the painter descends into a kind of lowliness that is unbelievably despicable. That Wesley, in his quiet heroism, ascends to a greater fate is a surprising and wonderful victory. 

Bainbridge, a seasoned British actor, and Jack Stokes, a rising young actor, have a seamless on-stage chemistry, switching roles, playing the other’s syphon as it were.  Bainbridge prevails and builds on his bullishness, first standing with his back to the audience, menacing the soldier with pistol posturing, until finally stricken, he falls. Meanwhile, Stokes’ Wesley remains an unequivocal challenger, quietly, albeit fiercely facing his antagonist. 

While there are no paintings or art of any kind on the walls of Lupine’s studio, Brian Morrell’s original score fills the space with musical interludes: marking silences, building the tension, overwhelming the senses. 

This production, named one of The Scotsman’s “Top Five Shows to See at the Edinburgh Fringe,” is part of 59E59 Theaters’ annual Brits off Broadway festival. A quick, intense drama, it fills the bill for positive sensation.

Shellshocked ****

By Paulanne Simmons

May 28, 2025: Lights Out: Nat ‘King’ Cole, the new jukebox musical by Colman Domingo and Patricia McGregor, is very different from other shows in its genre. In the first place, the show does not try to cover all, or even most of Cole’s life. It also doesn’t follow any chronological order. It is, as explained by Sammy Davis Jr (Daniel J. Watts), who is Cole’s “Beatrice” in this journey, a “fever dream.” This presents considerable challenges for McGregor, who also directs, which with the help of scenic designer Clint Ramos, she only partially overcomes.

Lights Out begins with Cole (Dulé Hill) in his dressing room, preparing for the final airing of The Nat ‘King’ Cole Show on NBC. The variety show is being cancelled because, although Rheingold Beer signed on as a regional sponsor, national sponsors were too afraid of the southern market to be associated with a show hosted by a black man. As Cole put it  “Madison Avenue is afraid of the dark.” 

Backstage musings and the onstage performances alternate throughout the 90-minute show. There are guest appearances by Eartha Kitt (Krystal Joy Brown), Betty Hutton (Ruby Lewis) and Peggy Lee (Lewis again), all performing Cole’s greatest hits. Even his daughter, Natalie (also Brown) shows up for a duet of “Unforgettable” with her father. Cole and Davis’s tap number to “Me and My Shadow,” which begins with the clicking of a typewriter, is breathtaking. 

Commercial breaks, projected on a screen and performed onstage are both delightfully amusing to watch and a penetrating commentary on life in America at that time. While Davis’s antics and constant needling are entertaining and provocative. Both Watts and Hill are excellent, but often McGregor lets Watts outshine Hill. 

However, the issues of racial bigotry and racial segregation often dwarf the story of Cole’s personal life. We hear about the murder of Emmett Till and the time Cole  was attacked by a group of white men while performing for an all-white audience at the Municipal Auditorium in Birmingham, Alabama. But the writers anachronistically include modern-day issues and battle cries, as when Natalie screams “I can’t breathe” after puffing on a cigarette the sponsors cram into her mouth. There are better ways to show how certain cigarette brands marketed to the black consumer.

On the other hand, the musical seems to gloss over many of Nat “King” Cole’s achievements. the King Cole Trio, a top selling group and the only black act on Capitol Records, became a model for small jazz groups. The Nat King Cole Show, was the first nationally broadcast television show hosted by a black American. Cole has a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame. At this time when our country is in such turmoil, it would be nice to see the glass half full once in a while.

By Isa Goldberg

May 27, 2025: A playful revival of William Inge’s 1955 play, Bus Stop, at Classic Stage Company makes for a cheerful confection. 

Watching the classic film starring Marilyn Monroe with a cast of movie idols – Don Murray, Arthur O’Connell, Betty Field, Eileen Heckart, Robert Bray, and Hope Lange, one would wonder what the ruckus was really all about. There are just too many emotional pratfalls, confusions, and misunderstandings – all brought to you with an overload of bluster. It feels a little too cartoon-like.

Truthfully, it was written at a time when pronouns were pronouns, and men were men…especially cowboys. In this production at CSC, no one could make that more of an imperative than the town sheriff, played with broad cowboy swagger by Đavid Lee Huynh, a strong actor with a rare bass voice. As it happens, he is of Vietnamese descent. Clearly not your stereotype of Matt Dillon, but it’s a beautiful evocation of that time, and that way of thinking that characterized America in the 50s, and it is truthful to our own time as well.

An interpreter of Inge’s work, director Jack Cummings has staged The Transport Group Theater Company’s,  Requiem for William – an evening of Inge’s one-acts, as well as The Dark at the Top of the Stairs. The latter, a grim tale of domestic life, turned raw and riveting in the Transport Group production in 2007.

Fortunately, Bus Stop, a play about love, invites a more comedic slice of life. Only love abates the loneliness of the small-town life Inge evokes – giving hope to the unhinged, the drunks, the homeless, the abandoned. Those characters are all here, waiting for the bus in a snowstorm, just like clowns waiting for Godot. 

Amidst this backdrop, Inge draws his picture of the American Dream, and what it means to the denizens of this small midwestern town. As Cummings’ program note explains, America “was desperate to believe in its own myth—the booming economy, the white picket fences, the technicolor dreams—Inge wrote the truth. These aren’t high-powered figures from big cities. They’re teachers, waitresses, doctors, housewives, bus drivers—ordinary people from small towns, whose pain and hope echo in all of us.”

At the center of it, Cherie (pronounced Cherry), a chanteuse in a small-town nightclub, feels as familiar to us as the girl next door. In this role, Midori Francis (Grey’s Anatomy) is simply believable. Convincing in her foibles, she is charming, despite trying so hard to remain self-possessed, and a wuss when it comes to romance. She’s adorable, and she’s our contemporary.

But even she realizes that her dreams of moving to Kansas City to work at the “hillbilly radio station” won’t ever happen. She imagines instead that she’ll wind up working at Leggett’s or Walgreens.

Driving her wild, beyond her dreams, Michael Hsu Rosen portrays Bo, the cowboy who loses his virginity to the nightclub singer and then abducts her. Carrying her off to his ranch in Montana, only to discover that she has had a lot more practice than him. Indeed, this Bo is one stung cowboy. Crying, and carrying on about the woman he so desperately loves, theirs is a happy ending. 

Not so for Bo’s dear friend Virgil, who raised him and taught him how to run a ranch. Moses Villarma demonstrates Virgil’s earnest loyalty to Bo, along with a sense of abandonment that explains his rootlessness.

Of course, it’s primarily Bo Decker who spurs the on-stage action. Rosen, an accomplished ballet dancer, brings a delicate physicality to the tough guy. His comedic twists and curls keep the story moving.

It’s clear from the get-go that this is going to be about the battle of the sexes. At the play’s opening, two waitresses prepare for the bus passengers to arrive. From their conversation we realize they have some negative feelings about men. The older of the two, Grace, played with graceful ease by Cindy Cheung, tries to hide her philandering lifestyle. As she imparts to her young employee Elma, making love is one thing, and being alone is another.

In this production, Delphi Borich portrays Elma Duckworth as both innocent and fully aware. In her relationship with the professor, Dr. Lyman, she reveals her vulnerability, as well as her love of literature, reading Romeo and Juliet with the old drunk, but never is she undone. Even pedophiles get some compassion. In this role, Rajesh Bose plays the downward spiraling arch of a real lost soul.

While the storm continues to rage outside, all the action takes place in Grace’s diner. Peiyi Wong’s scenic design, a turquoise bar with orange stools definitely reminds us of Howard Johnson’s, which achieved its hegemony in the 1950’s. Mariko Ohigashi’s costumes, from uniforms to cowboy boots and women’s dresses, are timeless. 

The production, a partnership between CSC, The Transport Group, and The National Asian American Theater Company, applauds our nation’s diversity.

Cummings’ vivid appreciation of Inge’s realism brings a refreshing sensibility to the stage, and a spark of light in the storm.

Bus Stop ***1/2

By David Sheward

May 26, 2025: There are several thrilling elements in Goddess, the new musical at the Public Theater, and in Lights Out: Nat “King” Cole, the new play with music at the New York Theater Workshop. But both shows fail to coalesce into a satisfying whole. Goddess features the exciting voice of Amber Iman, a vibrant score by Michael Thurber, and dazzling choreography by Darrell Grand Moultrie, but the book by Saheem Ali (who also directs) and Pulitzer Prize-winning playwright James Ijames (credited with “additional book material”) is cliched and underdeveloped. 

The plot revolves around the divine singer Nadira (a stunning Iman) who is in reality Marimba, goddess of music. Like the Rita Hayworth character in the Hollywood movie musical, Down to Earth, Marimba has descended from the heavens and experiences internal conflict when she falls in love with a mortal (a virile Austin Scott as Omari, the son of politician in modern-day Mombasa, the capital of Kenya). 

In order to fulfill her destiny as mankind’s muse, Marimba must defy her mother, the evil goddess of war (represented by a giant puppet beautifully designed by Julian Crouch). Similarly, Omari, who longs to expression himself as sax player, is forced to confront his conservative parents and veer from their plans for him to continue the family’s political dynasty. The authors fail to deliver on either of these fronts, denying us the battle for either character which will resolve their conflicts. Instead, their romance is cut short when Marimba returns skyward and all struggles are quickly wrapped up in a tidy finale. 

The ending and the tired plot are something of a let down, but there are plenty of musical pluses along the way. Iman is a divine vision with a soaring voice to match. Austin Scott makes an attractive equal as her leading man, skillfully depicting Omari’s inner conflict and he plays a mean sax. Nick Rashad Burroughs and Arica Jackson provide generous comic relief as saucy emcee and barmaid at Moto Moto, the nightclub where Nadira plies her trade. Destinee Rae as Omari’s ambitious fiancee, J Paul Nicholas as his oppressive father, and Ayana George Jackson as his loving mother do their best to bring life to their stereotyped roles. Reggie D. White is an intriguing, mystifying presence as a sagacious seer. Melissa Clark, Teshomech Olenja, and Awa Secka comprise the vibrantly sexy GrioTrio, an African Greek Chorus narrating the tale.

Thurber’s score combines elements of jazz, R&B, world music and Afro roots, pumping blood into the cliched storyline as does Moultrie’s exciting dances and Ali’s fluid direction. Arnulfo Maldonado’s imaginative set and Dede Ayite’s colorful costumes combine earthy and otherworldly elements as does Bradley King’s spectral lighting. Like its titular heroine, Goddess attempts to reconcile its heavenly and baser portions, but doesn’t bring a successful mixture off.

Similarly, Colman Domingo and Patricia McGregor’s Lights Out: Nat “King” Cole seeks to blend disparate components which don’t quite successfully coalesce. The goal here is to combine a conventional show-biz bio with stark political commentary. Co-authors Domingo and McGregor who also directs, set up the framework of the last taping of Cole’s NBC variety series on Dec. 17, 1957. The affable, chart-topping crooner was the first African-American to host a network series. The Peacock net has consigned it to the ratings desert of Saturday afternoons at 6:30 pm and finally is axing the series due to pressure from Southern affiliates who cannot tolerate a Black performer in a non-subservient role. 

Cole (the magnificently versatile Dulé Hill) has attempted to walk the racial tightrope of maintaining a dignified image while not stirring up racial resentments. As he prepares for his final broadcast, Domingo and McGregor throw Cole into a fever dream of nightmarish proportions. They cast Sammy Davis Jr. (an equally exciting Daniel J. Watts) as Cole’s explosive alter ego, demonically defying racist expectations and ripping up the staid musical numbers. The white-bread, white Christmas special becomes a broad political cartoon as racist tropes detonate and the backstage handlers blow their tops. Cole’s hits such as “Nature Boy,” “Somewhere Along the Way,”  “Straighten Up and Fly Right,” and “Smile” serve as springboards for editorialization on race relations.

Through numerous numbers, the political points are made and remade till it feels as if the authors are hitting us over the head. Fortunately, the musical arrangements, supervision and orchestrations by John McDaniel and music direction by Vadim Feichtner are superb. The highlight of the entire show is a titanic tap battle between Cole and Davis reminiscent of Savion Glover’s Bring in da Noise/Bring in da Funk, expressing the characters’ anger at social injustice. It starts with Cole typing to the tune of “I’m Gonna Sit Write Down and Write Myself a Letter” while Davis taps to “Me and My Shadow,” gradually the two tunes and dances blend together into a face-off of rhythmic rage. Jared Grimes created the dynamic tap choreography. 

McGregor’s direction is proficient but overheated, presenting the characters as symbols rather than flesh and blood. Hill and Watts deliver supernova performances, displaying impressive song-and-dance skills as well as liming the depths of these show-biz icons’ conflicted psyches. (The use of Davis of a representation of African-American anger is interesting since the real Davis was a political conservative, publicly embracing Richard Nixon and receiving criticism from Black progressives for his non-confrontational stance on race.) There are also impressive musical and dramatic portraits from Krystal Joy Brown as Eartha Kitt and Cole’s daughter Natalie, Ruby Lewis as white guests stars Betty Hutton and Peggy Lee, Kenita Miller as Cole’s mother, Kathy Fitzgerald as a veteran make-up artist, Christopher Ryan Grant as the TV show’s cynical producer, and Walter Russell III as the young Billy Preston and Cole as a kid. Clint Ramos’ TV studio set and Katie O’Neill’s period costumes capture the 1950s atmosphere. There is wit and dynamic musical talent in Lights Out, but its intense and unrelenting tone obscure and overstate its message.

Goddess ***

By Alix Cohen

May 25, 2025: Ogresse is a musical fable billed as “both a biomythography (weaving myth, history, and biography in epic narrative) and an homage to Erzulie”, the Haitian African spirit of love, beauty, and flowers; also jealous and spoiled. French/ Haitian/American Cécile McLorin Salvant has devised a dark, powerful tale of hunger, Diaspora, nature, love, and lies. 

Played by a 13 piece orchestra, the cantata features folk, country, baroque opera, and jazz; dramatically lyrical; dancey; dissonant. If at all familiar with the artist, you know she excels at all these genres and more. Vocal is astonishing, but Salvant doesn’t just sing, she’s viscerally possessed by her characters. A screen above offers intermittent, impressionistic animation. 

Majestic in an ochre silk robe, Salvant begins: “There is a woman lived in the woods on the outskirts of town/Her skin was chocolate brown/ Upon her head she wore a crown- of human bones…She lived with the birds…” Strings hum. Vibraphone shimmers. Imagine a magical playground.

“Songs of my beauty rolled down the hill and echoed through the valley/Father had flown away some time ago/My face was all he left behind/Mother remarried a shadow…” Oboe personifies. “The shadow took over our home/It swallowed mother and tried to put me in his mouth.” (her hands rise like claws) “I bit his head off …” The intended victim ran to the woods and waited for consequence.

A banjo plays. We see a small town on pink ground. The Ogresse “is vast/She opens her mouth/It’s the size of a planet/Vaster than the sea (arms extend wide.)/She’s bigger than a tree…” Vocal slip/slides. Trombone, bongos, and bass provide classical swing. Salvant holds her wrists and sways. “From a distance she looks like a bear/Beware…” Eyes pop, arms warn.

The town comes together to catch her- fiddle and banjo pervade- “but instead when they got there/She opened her mouth and put them inside…One man got away…” “A woman in the woods is feasting on your sons,” he cries. We see a willow tree and skulls. “I’m breezy/I do what I want, whatever I want,” the Ogresse sings, “Because I don’t have to shine anyone’s shoes…” Salvant swings back and forth sweetly grinning. Trumpet is jaunty. Banjo weighs in. Bass adds ballast.

The bemoans her loneliness. Who could possibly love someone like her?! Solo piano and French lyrics (alas, untranslated) emerge with moody jazz. 

A little girl named Lily ventures into the wood, despite father’s warning. The Ogresse is “beguiled by the curious, porcelain child.” Banjo, drums, violins; high, wispy vocal.  We see yellow grass and poppies, blue sky. It’s a country tune. Nature has its own demands. The gorgon’s stomach rumbles. 

“Hair like silk/Lips of blood (a yodel)/Skin so white it’s diaphanous…What is it about a white woman that does me in so?” Country rhythm launches a two-step. It grew dark, Lily walked into arms, then mouth, suddenly gone.” We see red shoes left at the edge of a tangled wood. Guitar, flute and bongos play mambo. Muted trumpet, keyboard, strings expand. There’s another French verse.

Lead by her father, the village calls for Lily. “Vengeance! Bounty!” they cry. One who does not join comes up with a plan. “I’m small and fearful. I have no upper body strength. They’re trying to kill the beast with force. I’ll kill her with kindness and love.” Vibraphone, drums, strings. “I’m not ambitious, but this is an opportunity.” We see giant flowers, milkweed seeds on the wind.

Like many myths and fairy tales, this one grows light, but ends in tragedy. The would be assassin prostrates himself declaring love, returning every day to speak and sing until the Ogresse believes. They dance. The birds know he lies, but can’t read his heart. She doesn’t listen until proof seems irrefutable. She doesn’t listen. Both die horrifically.

Lyrics are poetic, but never soft. Some repeat like chants. Twice we’re lead astray by hope, then betrayed. There’s timeless grandiosity to the story. Salvant might be a traveling minstrel performing before a riveted king. Her life could depend on the balance of attention. She sings with pride of skill and purpose of message.

Ogresse is in development to become an animated film directed by Salvant.

By Samuel L. Leiter

May 23, 2025: The Public Theater’s latest musical, Goddess, on the same stage that introduced A Chorus Line and Hamilton, bursts onto the stage with an electrifying energy that’s impossible to ignore. Loosely inspired by the African myth of Marimba—the goddess who transformed heartbreak into music—the production intertwines folklore, jazz, and contemporary musical theater to deliver a visually and sonically captivating experience. With music and lyrics by Michael Thurber and a book by director Saheem Ali (with additional material by James Ijames), Goddess makes its New York debut following a triumphant world premiere at Berkeley Repertory Theatre, offering audiences a rich, culturally resonant musical experience. Ali’s staging once more proves that he is among the most innovative American stage directors, whether for straight or musical drama.

Set against the backdrop of Moto Moto, a sultry Afro-jazz club in Mombasa, Kenya, the story follows Omari (Austin Scott), a young man grappling with the weight of familial expectations and personal dreams. Omari has returned home after studying in America, prepared to step into his father’s political legacy by running to replace his father as governor, while also fulfilling his engagement to his fiancée, Cheche (Destinee Rea). He keeps his great talent as a saxophone player secret from his family, however, because it clashes with his political ambitions in a society where popular music is frowned on by conservatives like his dad. However, his carefully structured future begins to unravel when he encounters Nadira (Amber Iman), a beguiling singer whose voice possesses an almost supernatural allure. Nadira, as it turns out, is more than a gifted performer—she is Marimba, the goddess of music, disguised and in hiding from her formidable mother, the goddess of evil, who threatens her with destruction if she doesn’t become the goddess of war.

The opening act of Goddess is an explosion of musical and choreographic brilliance, immersing audiences in a vivid and dynamic world. Thurber’s score seamlessly blends R&B, Afrobeat, pop, East African taarab, and jazz, crafting a rich soundscape that is at its strongest when celebrating joy and communal expression. The use of live instrumentation from an onstage band enhances the score’s depth, giving it an organic, immersive quality that heightens the emotional impact of the production.

The choreography, helmed by Darrell Grand Moultrie, is a mesmerizing display of movement and rhythm. Each step, turn, and gesture feels deeply rooted in cultural tradition while maintaining a contemporary fluidity, sometimes bordering on hip-hop, that keeps the energy fresh and vibrant. The dancers, whether engaged in ensemble numbers or intimate solos, radiate a sense of celebration and exuberance. Furthermore, the incorporation of African griots, native rituals, and puppetry adds authenticity to the storytelling, grounding the production in its mythological and cultural inspirations.

Goddess excels in its theatrical dynamism, but struggles under the weight of its second act’s shift toward introspection. As the narrative stresses its themes of duty versus personal expression, and the romantic relationship of Omari and Nadira ripens, the pacing slows, and the music loses much of its earlier vitality as emotional balladry assumes dominance over joie de vivre. While Amber Iman delivers consistently breathtaking vocals—her voice carrying an ethereal power that conveys both her character’s divinity and raw vulnerability—the songs become more uniform in tone, the variety and spontaneity that make the first act so compelling replaced by melodic monotony decorated with melisma and power notes.

The book, despite its ambitious themes, leans heavily into conventional storytelling tropes. Omari’s internal struggle, though well-acted by Austin Scott, falls into familiar territory, making the central conflict somewhat predictable. Nadira’s divine dilemma never fully explores the emotional stakes in a way that deepens our investment. The transition between acts loses the organic flow established in the opening, and it seems to take forever to resolve the situation as we plod toward what, by happy contrast, ends the show with a thrillingly explosive musical conclusion.

Regardless of its narrative flatness, Goddess’s stellar performances throb with life. Amber Iman dominates the stage with a commanding and celestial presence, her voice weaving together sorrow, seduction, and triumph. Austin Scott brings heartfelt sincerity and warmth to Omari, convincingly portraying a man caught between duty and destiny. Destinee Rea’s Cheche is fiery and resolute, making her passionately compelling.

Arica Jackson and Nick Rashad Burroughs—their contrasting physical types giving their pairing extra mileage—provide much-needed comedic relief as the subsidiary lovers, Rashida and Ahmed. Their performances serve as buoyant counterpoints to the main romance’s weightier aspects. Burroughs, in particular, showcases remarkable dexterity, using movement and expression to elevate his memorably comedic moments.

From a technical standpoint, Goddess delivers stunning visuals that heighten its exotic atmosphere. Arnulfo Maldonado’s set design brings Moto Moto to life, enveloping the audience in its warm, smoky ambiance. Dede Ayite’s vibrant costumes reflect Kenya’s cultural heritage while subtly distinguishing divine figures from their mortal counterparts. Bradley King’s versatile, complex lighting design plays an instrumental role in enhancing the mystical as well as romantic elements of the story.

While Goddess may resemble The Buena Vista Social Club in its celebration of music’s communal power within a threatening political environment, it stands apart because of its original score and mythological framework. Its greatest triumph lies in its ability to create moments of pure joy—those electrifying instances when the music, movement, and narrative fuse into something greater than the sum of their parts. If the production could sustain that energy throughout its entire runtime, Goddess might almost touch divinity.

Goddess *** 1/2

By David Sheward

May 18, 2025: When you walk into the Vineyard Theatre for Nazareth Hassan’s Bowl EP, a co-production between Vineyard and the National Black Theatre in association with The New Group, you’ll certainly be impressed with the elaborate set by Adam Rigg and Anton Volovsek. The entire playing space was converted into a empty swimming pool with the audience behind mesh fences on all four sides. According to the digital program we are “on the edge of an urban wasteland in the middle of the galaxy.”

The hollow bowl of the pool serves as a meeting place for two African-American wannabe rappers, the bisexual Quentavius da Quitter (Oghenero Gbaje), and the transgender female Kelly K. Klarkson (Essence Lotus). They are trying out their skateboarding and rhyming skills. Hassan’s jagged, fragmented script begins promisingly with short, sharp vignettes of Quentavius and Kelly alternating between brainstorming names for their rap group, skating, and flirting with each other through food. Quentavius suggestively offers Kelly a banana, an apple, and a sandwich. The scenes are punctuated with brief titles, or tracks as in a music album, in different type faces projected on the floor of the empty pool (Zavier Augustus Lee Taylor created the eye-popping video and projection design.)

The two grow gradually closer and slowly reveal their damaged past as they try out various meaning-laden catchphrases for their rap duo’s name (Dad’s Vomit, Dead Mothers, Michael Jackson’s Accusers). It’s almost as if they talking in code, hiding their true feelings. The dialogue is funny and tender, Hassan’s direction is well paced and subtly undercovers subtext as does the acting by Gbaje and Lotus. Gabje’s shift in tone from jovial wisecracking to sober recollection when the topic of sexual abuse is introduced is shattering. Plus the two are pretty nifty skateboarders.

But about half-way through the play’s 85 minutes, the proceedings take a bizarre turn and what started off as a moving love story of two alienated outsiders reaching out to each other through their love of rap and skateboarding turns into a confusing jumble. A third character pops out of an opening in the pool and takes over. She is dressed like a cosplay version of a Japanese anime character (DeShon Elem created the flashy costumes) and identifies herself as Lemon Pepper Wings. Presumably she represents Quentavius’ inner demons and dominates the action until the end of the play. She forces Quent and Kelly to live out their dreams by performing a rap concert. (Free Fool is credited with the intense infectious music.) Then Lemon Pepper performs an act of symbolic violence on the two (literally ripping their guts out) and explains their tragic fates in a powerhouse monologue. Felicia Curry delivers a stunning performance as this force of nature. She manages to convey the essence of longing, passion and self-hatred and still portray a credible character rather than a symbol.

Unfortunately, for the latter half of the play, Hassan tells us about the two rappers’ unhappy story instead of showing us. Lemon Pepper Wings’ long speech which is half abstract concepts and half storytelling, goes on too long and interest in Quentavus and Kelly is lost. The set and the skateboarding are fun, but they are not enough to maintain a fully-fleshed work.

Bowl EP **

By Paulanne Simmons

May 14, 2025: There’s something deliciously anarchistic about Fat Cat Killers, Adam Szymkowicz’s new play now at the Gene Frankel Theatre, under the direction of Andrew Block. The show, of course, deals with a serious subject: corporate greed and the indifference of CEOs, but the plot is so riotously ridiculous and the cast so joyously antic, the message goes down with a good deal of sugar. 

Two laid off workers, Steve (Christopher Lee) and Michael (David Carl), decide to  kidnap and capture their boss, CEO Dave Russell (Philip Cruise). But much like the characters in O. Henry’s “The Ransome of Red Chief,” they haven’t really figured out how they’re going to get the money and what they’re going to do with their victim. Unlike what happens in O. Henry’s story, their captive actually wants to assist his captors, on condition they’ll share the loot with him.

Considering how thin the plot is, it’s remarkable that the three actors can keep the audience engaged and laughing for almost ninety minutes. This is partly because Szymkowicz does provide several twists in his plot and Block knows how to keep the action moving. But it is mostly thanks to the cast, whose energy and commitment almost make up for the clumsiness of their acting.

If Steve and Michael were smarter, Dave more believable and the writing sharper, Fat Cat Killers might have been a biting satire. As it is, the comedy is more in the style of The Three Stooges, complete with a good deal of slapstick.

This is a low budge show, and Scott Fetterman’s set would benefit from scenery that contrasts the luxury of a corporate office with the dinginess of the  hideout where Steve and Michael keep their victim.

Fat Cat Killers goes on a bit too long, as we hear Steve’s manifesto, his retraction and finally the compromise he strikes. By the time the play ends, most of the comedy has evaporated.

Fat Cat Killers arrives fortuitously not that long after Luigi Mangione became infamous to some and a hero to others for killing UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson, but the play was actually written over a decade ago. In that sense it is remarkably prescient. 

Fat Cat Killers ***1/2

title.rendered: The Last Bimbo of the Apocalypse ****, All-Nighter ****

content.rendered:
By David Sheward

May 14, 2025: The impact of our celebrity-obsessed digital culture is explored in the intimate and funny new musical The Last Bimbo of the Apocalypse from The New Group at the Signature Theater Center. The book by Michael Breslin and Patrick Foley sharply satirizes the  click-crazy ecosphere which values appearance and flash over substance. The energetic rock score by Breslin (music and lyrics) and Foley (additional music and lyrics) captures the empty ache experienced by many Gen Z-ers seeking meaning through their devices. The show could have been as shallow as the situation it purports to parody, but the authors have captured the sweet innocence of an alienated youth, isolated by COVID and unable to recover in-person social skills. “I’ll take a picture on my phone/And post it so I’m not alone,” is one of the more haunting lyrics. “I don’t wanna do anything/And I want to be rewarded for it” is another which captures the desperate state of disconnection dominating our world.

The plot centers on an infamous picture of media sensations Lindsay Lohan, Britney Spears, and Paris Hilton which ran in the New York Post in 2006 with the caption “The Three Bimbos of the Apocalypse.” Breslin and Foley imagine there was a fourth “Bimbo” in the pic in the form of a barely visible wrist. An Internet sleuth calling herself “Brainworm” (a heartbreaking Milly Shapiro) is determined to find the identity of the missing girl. By searching for this elusive possible pop-culture icon, she hopes to find her own identity and possibly venture into real life. (She has not left her room in four years.) She is joined by a pair of gay male YouTubers identified as Bookworm and Earworm, one of whom is closeted (funny and flamboyant Patrick Nathan Falk and Luke Islam). 

Their search leads to Coco (dynamic Keri Rene Fuller), the wrist in the photo and a wannabe singer who vanished after her one attempt at topping the charts failed. Along the way, the trio encounters Coco’s religious-fanatic mother (fiery Sara Gettelfinger) and an unidentified friend (quirky Natalie Walker) who holds the key to the mystery. 

Director Rory Pelsue cleverly stages this journey through cyberspace as if the characters were all in physical proximity though they are mostly communicating through their screens. Amit Chandrashaker’s spectral lighting, some of which is through cell-phone illumination, aides in the illusion. Cole McCarty designed the kicky costumes spanning the last two decades of hipster fashion. Pelsue also balances the comic, satiric elements with compassion for the disillusioned Internet addicts. The cast, especially Shapiro, portrays them as broken loners rather than as eccentric goofballs obsessed with trivia. These are more than comic Bimbos, they’re human beings.

In another Off-Broadway show about young people coping with a difficult world, Natalie Margolin’s All-Nighter insightfully dissects a quintet of female college seniors as they pull their final nocturnal study session and embark on becoming adults. Each is riddled with anxiety and insecurities as they down copious amounts of Adderall, energy drinks, white wine, and humus to maintain the stamina to complete their last assignments. A ghost is blamed for unusual happenings in their shared house as the night drags on and uncomfortable truths are revealed. 

Margolin is a promising playwright, creating believable characters and skillfully building a riveting story arc employing interesting details and building suspense through careful clues. Jaki Bradley’s well-paced direction includes hilariously fast-motion action to denote the passage of time and Isa Briones, Kathryn Gallagher, Alyah Chanelle Scott and understudy Tessa Albertson deliver complex portraits of young women in conflict with themselves and each other. As Wilma, the outspoken outsider of the group, Julia Lester crashes into the action like a hurricane. Wilma longs to be noticed, and more importantly, accepted. Lester fulfills this objective with spectacular character choices, endowing each gesture and action with subtext. Even munching on a bag of potato chips or aggressively opening a collapsible stool so she can join the study table reveals tons about Wilma and her needs. It’s a fascinating performance in an excellent ensemble.

The Last Bimbo of the Apocalypse ****

title.rendered: THE LAST BIMBO OF THE APOCALYPSE **1/2

content.rendered:
By Samuel L. Leiter

May 13, 2025: In an era where, as they say, nostalgia is currency and irony king, The Last Bimbo of the Apocalypse arrives at the Pershing Square Signature Center with as much subtlety as Barbra Streisand at a whispering contest. This world-premiere musical arrives courtesy of The New Group, which usually offers nonmusical plays with one or more starry actors. It obviously appealed to the youthful audience members when I attended (standing O? Natch), but it was decidedly ho-hum hokum for this jaded reviewer.

Last Bimbo takes inspiration from a 2006 tabloid photo featuring Paris Hilton, Lindsay Lohan, and Britney Spears—infamously dubbed “The Three Bimbos of the Apocalypse.” A placard featuring the original New York Post photo and article gree ts visitors in the lobby of the Alice Griffin Jewel Box Theatre. But the show’s Gen Z protagonists aren’t interested in those well-documented icons; they’re on a mission to uncover the identity of the mysterious fourth woman in the frame, whose hand and nothing else is seen on Hilton’s shoulder. A bit of sleuthing reveals she’s Coco (Keri René Fuller), a (fictional) one-hit wonder who vanished from pop history.

The book, by Michael Breslin and Patrick Foley, is a fever dream of internet detective work, celebrity obsession, and musical theater overkill. It’s almost like a poor sister of an “Only Murders in the Building” podcast, with its three Sherlock wannabes standing in for Steve Martin, Martin Short, and Selena Gomez. The direction, by Rory Pelsue, leans into the chaos, embracing a theatrical style that quivers between kitschy satire and desperate melodrama. The result is an unsatisfying production that is rarely visually arresting, even less often satirically insightful, and, when all is said and done, overtly tiresome.

Stephanie Osin Cohen’s neon-highlighted set design is a bandstand like arrangement of several receding arches, the upstage ones allowing for drop curtains to be slotted in with scenic images. For some scenes, the five-piece band, supplemented by two playback engineers, is visible in the upstage space. Scenic units are rare, the acting area being mostly free of specificity. Although colorfully lit by Amith Chandrashaker, its general blandness offers little to a book that plays more like a revue than a conventional musical. The frequent, if inconsistent, presence of brightly colored, handheld mics only serves to emphasize the innocuousness of the proceedings. Cole McCarty’s costumes, at least, have fun with Y2K looks, displaying enough rhinestones to make Destiny’s Child blush.

The talented ensemble does its best to navigate the tonal whiplash. Heading the trio of investigative young fans, virtual recluses who spend their lives online, is Brainworm (Milly Shapiro), her enthusiastic companions being the flamboyantly gay Earworm (Luke Islam), and the, for the moment, sexually uncertain, ultra-nerdy Bookworm (Nathan Patrick Falk); they bring energy and commitment to their roles, even when the script leaves them stranded in a sea of pop-culture references. Sara Gettelfinger plays Coco’s mother, and Natalie Walker—who has some rather unusual vocal skills—is Coco’s sister, Kiki. They’re all good enough to deserve better than the cartoons to which they’re reduced in this campy attempt at satirizing celebrity worship.

And then there’s the music. Breslin and Foley’s score is undeniably rhythmic and energetic, but much of it feels like a playlist of vaguely familiar, but unoriginal familiar pop hooks. The electronic-heavy arrangements pulse with life, yet rarely linger in the memory. And Megumi Katayama and Ben Truppin-Brown’s sound design fails to sharpen the words and lyrics when those portable mics come kissing-close to actors’ mouths.

The Last Bimbo of the Apocalypse struggles to find a consistent voice. It wants to be a biting satire, a heartfelt tribute, and a raucous spectacle all at once. Instead, it often feels like a musical that’s trying too hard to be in on the joke.

Is it entertaining? Sometimes. Is it tiresome? Often. Is it worth seeing? Well, that depends on your tolerance for cardboard characters obsessed with uncovering a piece of extreme trivia in a world of campy, gay-oriented excess set to an uninspired score. I admit, though, it has a great title.

The Last Bimbo of the Apocalypse **1/2

480 W. 42nd Street NYC.
Running time: 90 mins. no intermission. thenewgroup.org

By Alix Cohen

May 12, 2025: “Anything inanimate that you animate is a puppet.” Basil Twist

How does a program like HERE’s Dream Music Puppetry (producer of Puppetopia) get started in a country without traditions that historically evolved in Europe? This particular “Once Upon a Time” begins with the rather enchanted trajectory of master practitioner, Basil Twist. (Yes, that’s his real name.)

Speaking to the artist is infectiously pleasurable. He makes every discovery en route come as alive as his fanciful, fabricated characters. Though highly experienced and respected, Basil maintains an enviable sense of curiosity and wonder. He misses hands on work when asked only to design and/or direct.

One might say Basil Twist was born to the métier of puppeteer. His maternal grandfather, dance bandleader Griff Williams, had such love of the art that he commissioned hand carved, wood marionettes of well known bandleaders and musicians with which he performed during shows. Griff would rise from the piano and manipulate a figure as a band instrument supplied sound.

Video of Griff Williams. Courtesy of Basil Twist.

Basil’s mother inherited a penchant for animating figures. When he was growing up in San Francisco, she was one of a group of women who put on amateur shows in hospitals and at parties. Hand puppets were the rage. Basil was often backstage. “It made a big impression on me.”

The boy gravitated to Fisherman’s Wharf to watch popular street performer Bob Hartman and repeatedly asked to be taken to Children’s Fairyland, a kind of amusement park in Oakland, California with a permanent puppet theater. He had his own first theater at three, creating characters out of paper.

Destiny made itself known when Basil was ten years-old. His dad built him a real theater, grandmother Dorothy gifted him Griff’s marionettes and, on a family trip to New York, Basil was invited to The Sesame Street Muppet Workshop through connections.

Seeing his enthusiasm, Henson’s people recommended the family go to a then current show by French puppeteer Philippe Genty who specialized in abstract work – “fabric and strange shapes that were transformed.” Perhaps this was the seed for Basil’s own Symphony Fantastique, featuring cloth that dances under water evoking sea creatures.

Basil was shy in grade school and used puppetry to deflect. He made elaborate Halloween costumes sometimes never worn and gave a book report on ancient Greece using a dog costumed in a toga and laurel wreath, inadvertently garnering extra credit. With high school, puppetry felt too feminine. The teenager stopped making characters and put the craft aside.

The briefest stay at Oberlin College found him looking desperately for stimulation at The Alternative Studies Department. Lo and behold, a volume “fell open at The Center for Puppetry Arts in Atlanta which had an internship program.” Basil applied.

Meanwhile, he came to New York and took courses at NYU. “Under the cloak of being a student,” the young man looked under “P” in the phone book and volunteered everywhere the art was practiced. He hung around the tear-down of a Julie Taymor exhibit at The Library for the Performing Arts, made her acquaintance, and acted the bird in her production of Juan Darién: A Carnival Mass.

Atlanta followed. Then France. Basil learned about and applied to L’École nationale supérieure des arts de la marionette in Charleville-Mézières, the puppetry capital of Europe and the home of The World Puppet Festival. Steeped in tradition, the institution rigorously taught history, technique, design, costuming, dramaturgy, music, acting…He bucked at its conservative outlook, but was the only American ever to graduate.

Back in New York, the young artist immersed himself in the lively gay nightlife scene of lower Manhattan. He performed in bars and nightclubs, helped drag performers and worked with other companies. “That was a whole other education.” This eventually took him to HERE Arts Center where he acted with Mabou Mines as the hind legs of Rose, the dog.

When a show he’d made with a friend in France looked for a New York venue, he asked at HERE. “They said, we have this downstairs storage room we’ve always wanted to be a theater…So we got some folding chairs and put up a curtain. It was fun.”

HERE asked whether Basil would like to do something else. The OBIE-award winning Symphony Fantastique was developed. “It became a project. We had to get the new theater up to code. The piece officially opened downstairs. It had an EXIT sign and all the stuff you need.”

“There was a lot of fundraising necessary. Part of what you do is ask family and friends. Somewhere in there my grandmother Dorothy gave money, not really a big donation, but a solid gesture. Suddenly the space got named The Dorothy B. Williams Theatre or, as we call it, Dot. I never requested it. The theater opened with a party. Dorothy came in a wheelchair and cut a ribbon. She had Cancer at the time, so having a theater named after you…”

Outside the small theater in a display case, Griff Williams remarkable marionettes watch over of a theater named after his wife, helmed by his grandson.

Ben Brantley of The New York Times raved about Symphony Fantastique which, expected to run a couple of weeks, stayed up over a year and a half. “It was like, what are we going to do now?” Basil said. “I knew all these puppeteers. I had knowledge and access.”

Dream Music Puppetry was founded as one of the few programs in the country to grow and commission contemporary, adult puppet works, providing opportunities to puppet artists, encouraging multidisciplinary collaboration to develop new puppetry techniques.

There’s no formality to Basil’s position as artistic director, but once a year in December, Dot puts on Puppet Parlor, a one or two night cabaret with puppets and once a year each spring, it mounts Puppetopia with guest companies. Really the whole story is magical.

Puppetopia 2025

The Harlem Doll Palace May 21-June 1, 2025. Created by Alva Rogers, directed by Ashley Winkfield. Behind the pink door of a three story Harlem brownstone lies a world created by Lennon Holder Hoyte – affectionately known as Aunt Len. The dolls from her “dollection” seek to keep her, their beloved museum founder, alive before the outside world can invoke its realities of life, ashes and dust.

Rhynoceron, May 21-25, 2025 Directed and designed by KT Shivak. A puppetry show that traces true events surrounding the arrival of a one-horned rhinoceros to Renaissance Europe, sparking an obsession that continued for hundreds of years. A life size rhino puppet transforms in front of our eyes from a natural inspiring wonder to an object of human greed. 

Variations On (the) Water created by Lake Simmons. A poetic solo puppet performance that invites the audience to imagine and co-create a story embodying the sea, exploring its movement, vastness, poetry, and ability to saturate, flow, carry, drown, and nourish. Thursday, May 29, and Friday, May 30 at 8:30 p.m., Saturday, May 31 at 4 p.m., and 8:30 p.m., and Sunday, June 1 at 4 p.m.

Opening: Left to right: Harry James, Griff Williams ( his grandfather), Cab Calloway,Toscanini,

By Paulanne Simmons

May 6, 2025: If you thought all Irish plays are dark and depressing, think again. Irishtown, by Ciara Elizabeth Smyth may be one of the funniest plays of the season. It’s making its word premiere at the Irish Repertory Theatre. Directed by Nicola Murphy Dubey, the comedy features a stellar ensemble cast with perfect timing and excellent synergy.

When the play opens, we see the members of a Dublin theater company, veteran actor Constance (Kate Burton), ambitious rising star Síofra (Saoirse-Monica Jackson) and the opinionated Quin  (Kevin Oliver Lynch) rehearsing a play for a New York run. The play was written by lesbian playwright Aisling  (Brenda Meaney), based on a personal experience of sexual assault, and is directed by Poppy  (Angela Reed), a Brit with a checkered past. 

From the beginning, the actors have problems with the play. Their principal issue is that the play is not Irish enough. It’s set in England. It has no Irish accents. They are convinced the Yanks won’t like it. But they also have problems with each other. Quin and Constance exchange barbs on each other’s acting ability. Poppy, who is sort of married, begins an affair with Siofra, who is in a relationship with Aisling.

At the end of act one, they become so obnoxious Aisling marches off and leaves them without a play. This puts the company in a bind because if they don’t bring a play to New York City, they will owe the producers $250,000 in advance ticket sales. 

In order to save their company, the actors and director need to come up with a play. But they want to make sure it’s Irish. In one hilarious scene after another they define what an Irish play should be about: incest, ghosts, peasants, pigs, potatoes, the perfidy of the British. Most of all the ending cannot be happy. Each of the actors creates a scene that ends up being something very close to Aisling’s.

Anyone who has ever seen an Irish play will recognize the spoofs. At one point Quinn delivers his lines while stuck in an urn, à laBecket. The comedy is broad but so will be your smile.

Irishtown ****
Irish Repertory Theatre, 132 W 22nd St, NYC.
Running time: 90 minutes with no intermission. irishrep.org

title.rendered: JUST IN TIME ****, FLOYD COLLINS **1/2, ALL THE WORLD’S A STAGE  ****

content.rendered:
By David Sheward

May 5, 2025: The 2024-25 Broadway season closes out with a pair of wildly divergent musicals featuring stunning star turns by two of the musical theater’s brightest stars. Jonathan Groff is a true triple threat, singing, dancing, and acting his ass off as the tragically short-lived legendary crooner Bobby Darin in Just in Time while Jeremy Jordan goes to the opposite extreme, delivering an inspiring vocal and dramatic performance as a Kentucky cave explorer trapped in one position underground in Lincoln Center Theater’s revival of Floyd Collins. While Groff and Jordan are flawless, their shows vary in intent and execution. Just in Time is pure entertainment while Floyd Collins is muddled in its messaging.

The creatives behind Just in Time could have built the show following a familiar blueprint. Bobby Darin was a magnetic pop superstar who briefly challenged Sinatra and Presley as king of all media. He was a teen-idol recording and movie star in his 20s, but his weak heart lead to an early death at 37. Warren Leight and Isaac Oliver’s book is somewhat melodramatic, but focuses on celebrating Darin’s phenomenal talent, largely with humor. Their clever format stages Darin’s meteoric rise and tragic fall as a floor show (Ted Chapin is credited with the original concept). Set designer Derek McLane has exquisitely refitted the Circle in the Square as a glamorous 1950s nightclub complete with cabaret-style tables. Director Alex Timbers and choreographer Shannon Lewis have staged the proceedings with speed and ingenuity. Scenes of Darin’s chaotic show-biz and personal life are interspersed with spectacular numbers he made famous such as the title tune from Bells Are Ringing, “Mack the Knife,” “Splish Splash” and “Dream Lover,” beautifully orchestrated by Andrew Resnick and Michael Thurber.

In order for this gimmick to work, you need a supremely gifted star and Groff is it. He grabs the audience from his first breathtaking entrance, emerging from beneath McLane’s gorgeous bandstand on an elevator. He is introduced not as Darin, but in his own person. Then he jokes about the setting (“I love playing the basement of Wicked”), explains the premise, and then seamlessly launches into the first exuberant number, establishing this will be a fun evening, not a dark dirge. Groff is amazing, soulfully and energetically putting across song after song, executing Lewis’ razzle-dazzle dance steps and delivering a fully-realized portrait of the charming, brash, arrogant, yet lovable Darin.

But this is not a one-man show. Groff is supported by a sterling ensemble. Gracie Lawrence exhibits impressive pipes as Connie Francis, Darin’s first love and fellow chart-topper. As his wife Sandra Dee, Erika Henningsen conveys the depth beneath the Gidget-next-door image. Michele Pawk strikes sparks as Polly, his tough-as-nails mother, and Emily Bergl impressively doubles as his sister who has a family secret and as Sandra’s protective mother. Joe Barbara, Lance Roberts and Caesar Samayoa excel in multiple roles while Valeria Yamin, Christine Cornish, and Julia Grondin dazzle as a trio of showgirls, exquisitely outfitted by costume designer Catherine Zuber, who serve as a kind of Vegas Greek chorus.

Just in Time just wants us to have a great time and succeeds, but Floyd Collins tries to impart too many themes and leaves us confused. Originally presented Off-Broadway in 1996 for a brief run by Playwrights Horizons in their tiny theater (they’ve since moved to more spacious digs), Collins features a memorable, lush score by Adam Guettel, but a muddled book by Tina Landau who also directed and provided additional lyrics. She has staged the current revival which feels lost in the cavernous Vivian Beaumont. The plot focuses on the true story of the title character, an enterprising young explorer who became trapped in an underground tunnel while seeking a natural cavern to exploit for tourism in poverty-stricken 1925 Kentucky.

It’s not clear what Landau is trying to say here. Is it that the burgeoning media circus surrounding Floyd’s plight foretells our modern exploitative pop culture? Is that dreamers are crushed by corporations as Floyd is crushed by rocks? (The federal government eventually takes over the land Floyd sought to develop as an attraction.) Is it that Floyd’s big ambitions are at odds with his farmer father who can’t understand why he wants to crawl under the ground instead of growing crops above it. Landau introduces several messages and as a result none emerges clearly.

Landau has also dug herself into a hole, figuratively as well as literally. Once Floyd is trapped after the expositional first number, apart from fantasy and flashback sequences, he is stationary throughout the rest of the show. Guettel gives him long, reflective arias to warble while immobile and flat on his back. Despite being sung by the magnificently expressive Jeremy Jordan, several minutes from these solos could be cut without losing any impact.

Jordan does yeoman’s work in the challenging title role, delivering a rainbow of colors to Floyd’s passionate yearning, nostalgic recollections with his brother Homer, and his special connection to his sister Nelly, recently discharged from an asylum. But even he cannot overcome the show’s shortcomings. The mobile cast members worthy of praise are Jason Gotay’s earnest Homer, Lizzy McAlpine’s heartbreaking and sweet Nellie, Taylor Trensch’s compassionate reporter Skeets Miller, Marc Kudisch’s conflicted father, Jessica Molaskey’s caring stepmother, and Sean Allen Krill’s overbearing engineer.

As a director, Landau does her best to bring vibrant life to this confused, static story, but doesn’t quite make it. Lighting designer Scot Zielinski masterfully transforms the suggestive set by the design team dots into Floyd’s labyrinthine underground maze.

Off-Broadway, a smaller-scale musical attempts to put across a timely take on a relevant issue and largely has positive, if somewhat preachy results. All the World’s a Stage, presented by Keen Company at Theater Row Theater, employs a sparkling cast and tuneful orchestra of four each to tell the tale of a gay high school teacher in 1990s rural Pennsylvania reaching out to a misfit student through their mutual love of the theater. Adam Gwon’s score is enchanting and clever while his book is mostly heartfelt if occasionally reminiscent of an Afterschool Special in its overearnestness. Jonathan Silverstein’s staging steers clear of stereotypes and moves smoothly with flowing transitions. Matt Rodin movingly portray Rick, the closeted teacher. Jon-Michael Reese juggles flamboyance with fierceness as Michael, his boyfriend and the owner of queer-friendly bookshop. Elizabeth Stanley pours tons of emotion into the role of a supportive school secretary, but would she be bursting in copious tears over the plight of a work acquaintance? As Sam (short for Samantha) the alienated student, Eliza Pagelle is the find of this show. She runs the proverbial gamut from rebellious brat to shattered loner in song and speech. She’s the heart of this heartfelt intimate piece, a musical celebrating the love of the stage.

By Paulanne Simmons

April 30, 2025: The main artifice of Justin in Time, the new jukebox musical about Bobby Darin, is that it’s all artifice. The first thing Jonathon Groff says as he strides onto Derek McClane’s nightclub set at Circle in the Square Theatre is that he’s Jonathan Groff, an entertainer. He sings in the voice of Jonathan Groff. He tells us he sweats and spits a lot and we’re going to see a very wet show. He apologizes to his fellow-actors.

Only after this introduction does Groff tell us he is going to portray Bobby Darin, but even during the show there are many winks and nods letting us know that we don’t really have to suspend disbelief. Characters snap their fingers to stop time. They correct each other’s stories. But somehow, thanks to Groff’s magnetic presence , Alex’s Timbers wily direction, and the excellent supporting cast, we totally believe, as the show follows Darin’s life starting with his inauspicious birth in East Harlem to his death at 37.

Darin was a sickly kid the doctors didn’t expect to survive past 16, but the woman he thinks is his mother, the former vaudevillian Polly Walden (the gritty and appealing Michelle Pawk), and the woman he thinks is his sister, Nina (the emotionally charged Emily Bergl), work hard to prevent that from happening. Polly encourages him to develop his talents, and Darin becomes a songwriter for Connie Francis (the very likable Gracie Lawrence), but it’s when “Splish-Splash” becomes a hit that his career takes off.

Bobby falls in love with Connie but loses her to the wrath of her old-fashioned Italian father. The next girl he meets is his future wife, Sandra Dee (Erika Henningsen, who knows the difference between sweet and troubled). We see them fall in love, marry and divorce. After his divorce Bobby considers entering politics, but when Nina tells him the truth about his parents, he decides to work for Robert Kennedy. After Kennedy is assassinated, he goes into a deep depression. His comeback is short-lived.

Throughout the story of Darin’s life, it is the music that matters. Backed by the Sirens (Valeria Yamin, Christine Cornish, Julia Grondin), Groff sings many of Darin’s most famous songs (“Splish Splach,” “Mack the Knife,” “Lazy River”). Some of these songs are integrated into the action. But other songs were never sung by Darim; Lawrence sings Connie Francis’s hit “Who’s Sorry Now?” And some of the songs that were sung by Darin are sung by others in the show; Pawk sings a moving version of “Beyond the Sea.”

Warren Leight and Isacc Oliver’s book does not go into all the details of Darin’s life, or the life of those around him. It’s not clear exactly what happened to his marriage, what kind of relationship he had with his child or if he ever reconciled with his sister/mother.

But none of that really matters. As Groff tells us at the very beginning, the show is about a performer who wanted, above all else, to be loved by the audience. It’s clear Groff identifies with Darin. He wants the show to entertain. And so it does.

Just In Time *****
Circle in the Square 1633 Broadway, NYC.
Running time: two hours and 25 mins. including intermission. justintimebroadway.com

By Samuel L. Leiter

May 3, 2025. In recent seasons, Jonathan Groff, now 40 but still boyishly handsome, has become Broadway’s definition of a modern musical matinee idol, masculine yet gay, singing with tenderness and power, dancing with refinement and exuberance, acting with lighthearted charm and deep emotion, and playing the piano (not to mention, briefly, the drums) with all the frantic velocity of Jerry Lee Lewis. In Just in Time, a jukebox homage to Bobby Darin now at the Circle in the Square, he harnesses his multi-threat talents into a performance that is part impression, part confession, and entirely memorable.

Groff (Merrily We Roll Along), rising on an elevator trap, opens the evening not with a finger snap but with a memory of his own, not Darin’s. As a child in Pennsylvania’s Amish country, he tells us, he once performed in his mother’s pumps to a Bobby Darin record, a telling anecdote that both prefigures and defines the show’s hybrid tone. This is not a bio-musical in the style of Jersey Boys or Beautiful; it’s part cabaret and part memoir, the parts sometimes not perfectly harmonized under Alex Timbers (Beetlejuice)manically elegant direction.

Circle in the Square has been reconfigured by five-star designer Derek McClane into a three-quarter-round environment, with a Copacabana-style bandstand-style stage occupying the far end. The space within the U-shaped auditorium is filled with cabaret tables, evoking the smoke-filled glamour of a mid-20th-century nightclub. With the action popping up not only on stage but in every corner of the theatre, Justin Townsend’s lighting sends beams hither and yon, creating moody, sculptural effects, throwing long shadows and bursts of color onto the sprawling acting area. If you feel like you’ve wandered into a memory, the approach is definitely working.

The premise has Groff being both himself and the character he’s playing. He sings Darin’s greatest hits—“Splish-Splash,” “Beyond the Sea,” “Mack the Knife,” and, of course, “Dream Lover”—in mostly upbeat tempos, highly amplified, recalling Darin’s aura of a supercool, finger-snapping, 60’s swinging crooner. Darin—born Walden Robert Cossatto to an Italian-American family in the 1936 Bronx—had ambitions to be the next Frank Sinatra.

What we see is a Sinatra on steroids, down to the rakish tilt of his fedora, his every wrist flap accompanied by a loud, percussive beat. Sinatra only rarely danced, and Darin was more inclined to lithe, rhythmic movement when he sang (think a restrained Mick Jagger in a tux); he did not however perform Broadway-style choreography, as does Groff when he struts the vibrant terpsichore created for the show—despite rather confined spaces—by Shannon Lewis. Much of her flashy jazz and jive movement incorporates a gorgeous trio of identically dressed, long-legged “Sirens,” Valeria Yamin, Christine Cornish, and Julia Grondin.

Timbers’s direction uses the sprawling space to create as much of an immersive experience as possible, with action going on in the aisles, at the cabaret tables, and so forth, often only inches from spectators’ joyous faces. This approach has much appeal during the two-character scenes, but when the book (by Warren Leight and Isaac Oliver) requires extended dramatic expression, it sometimes clashes with the cabaret atmosphere, especially when furniture has to be pushed onto the bandstand stage for domestic drama.

This back and forth from straightforward musical numbers to biographical reenactments with family members may be important for narrative clarity but the overall concept doesn’t always embrace it with affection. And, given Darin’s family issues (a big reveal shocks him when he learns the identity of his real mother) and marital problems with Sandra Dee (Erika Henningsen), not to mention his professional and political concerns, there’s a lot—perhaps too much—that needs to be tucked in whenever the music stops. It’s a dilemma that most bio-musicals never fully solve; at least the musical numbers, some of which are placed to relate to what’s happening in Darin’s life, are terrifically arranged (by Andrew Resnick) and performed.

Catherine Zuber’s goodlooking costumes range from tailored suits for the star to pastiche versions of period everyday wear for him and everyone else. The chorus girls/Sirens get to wear a panoply of flashy, abbreviated showgirl costumes, a particular highlight coming in a scene at Portofino when these three beauties appear in straw sunhats, sunglasses, and bright frocks, as if they just stepped off a Vogue cover from the 1950s. I couldn’t keep count of how many changes they made, but they never failed to match their dancing with eye-candy appeal. Kudos as well to Tom Watson for his wig and hair designs.

Among the supporting players, Erika Henningsen’s Sandra Dee is poised and affecting, although her resemblance to the doll-faced teen movie star is slight. Gracie Lawrence, portraying Connie Francis, projects warmth and spark, and shows off her silver pipes with a heartrending “Who’s Sorry Now,” although, for those who grew up listening to the original, it can’t replace the real thing (seen here in one of several YouTube clips). Veteran Michele Pawk still rocks in the role of Darin’s grandmother Polly, capturing her Bronx accent and personality, supplemented by her rich vocal chops. Emily Bergl plays Darin’s presumed sister, and other roles, with versatility, while Joe Barbara, Caesar Samayoa, and Lance Roberts do yeoman service in multiple roles each.

But the guy driving this musical bus is Jonathan Groff, expressively volcanic, even though his lava famously erupts as saliva and sweat; my daughter proudly claimed to have been singed. This is about the most intense male performance around right now, equaling the kind of theatrical TNT female stars like Audra McDonald and Nicole Scherzinger are blowing up on other Broadway stages. And he does it practically nonstop for nearly two and a half hours, followed by a curtain call mini-concert of him and the cast reprising several songs.

I must add that the immersive design has unintended consequences. Those seated along the sides of the stage (I was at the top of the U near stage right) are frequently treated to actors’ sides and backs, obstructed sightlines, or awkward angles that obscure key interactions. One understands the allure of the three-quarters format for a cabaret-style show, and it was fun for a while to be so close to the action (if not to the band, as anyone seated near the musicians at an affair knows), but visitors may wish to check where they’re sitting beforehand in case they prefer a broader view of the proceedings.

Finally, the night I went I was struck by how many young women were glamorously dressed, as if attending a gala rather than a Broadway musical. Perhaps it speaks to the nostalgic power of Darin’s music, or to the enduring fantasy of Old New York nightlife. Sitting there in my jeans and polo shirt, I felt quite outclassed.

Just in Time should be around for a while. Jonathan Groff’s incandescence, the show’s handsome look, its immersive concept, and its robust sequence of exciting numbers, most of them golden oldies, are undeniable. Its combination of biodrama and juke box musical, however, remains an awkward one. Just in time, though, you ignore such things when the topnotch, 11-member band gets into it, and Groff opens his mouth, snaps his fingers, flicks his wrists, taps his feet, pounds the ivories, and lets the spittle fly.

Just In Time ****1/2
Circle in the Square 1633 Broadway, NYC.
Running time: two hours and 25 mins. including intermission. justintimebroadway.com
April 23 — November 30, 2025.
