title.rendered: REAL WOMEN HAVE CURVES: THE MUSICAL **1/2

content.rendered:
By Samuel L. Leiter

May 2, 2025. In a season low on original musicals that spotlight underrepresented voices (The Buena Vista Social Club excepted), Real Women Have Curves: The Musical arrives at the James Earl Jones Theatre with commendable ambition. Based on Josefina López’s 1990 play and the 2002 HBO film adaptation, the musical—which premiered at Cambridge’s American Repertory Theater in 2023—is set in 1987 East Los Angeles. It promises an empowering story of Latina womanhood, body positivity, immigrant fears, and female solidarity.

Regardless of these aspirations, Lisa Loomer and Nell Benjamin’s stage adaptation—directed and choreographed by Tony winner Sergio Trujillo—rarely achieves dramatic lift. The seams are visible in nearly every aspect of the production, from the trivialities of its book to its improbable plot and emotionally unearned climaxes. Even its talented cast of newcomers and veterans can’t salvage the wreckage.

There are at least three plot lines, loosely connected to a budding romance. First, we have the fight for survival of a dressmaking sweatshop owned by Estela (Florencia Cuenca), where her five female workers—soon joined by a sixth—are all undocumented immigrants in constant fear that the immigration authorities will come banging down the door. One plot line requires the arrest of a worker, Itzel (Aline Mayagoitia), giving us a bitter taste of what, at least in 1987, such persons had to endure at the hands of the authorities. (ICE wasn’t founded until 2003.) 

The show’s topicality makes it distinctive among recent musicals; immigration is a subject worthy of a full-scale serious musical. Here, though, it mainly adds context to more pressing dramatic issues, such as whether the dressmakers can fulfill a contract for 200 dresses needed by an imperious garment business entrepreneur named Mrs. Wright (Monica Tulia Ramirez). With so much at stake for the shop if they don’t deliver by a specified date—failure means they won’t get paid—it’s hard to reconcile the pressure they’re under with all the time they hang around schmoozing, singing, and dancing to fulfill the demands of musical theatre.

Then there’s the story of 18-year-old Ana García (Tatianna Córdoba), a bright Mexican-American teenager who works as a journalist for a local paper, and who’s won a scholarship to study writing at Columbia in New York. Her feisty, immigrant mother, Carmen (Justina Machado), resists, insisting Ana stay home and work in the family’s struggling garment factory. While family ties and financial concerns could certainly cause a flareup over this problem, the show, as a friend of mine forcibly argued, forces us to accept that a working-class immigrant mother, instead of shouting her pride out the windows, would insist her daughter abandon a freebee to the Ivy League so she can stay home and run a sewing machine. Although her father, Raul (Mauricio Mendoza), is more sympathetic to Ana’s dilemma, even his approval seems forced. 

Similarly questionable within this world is the insistence that Ana must go to Columbia, with no thought given to the many excellent universities in Southern California. If she’s smart enough to land a scholarship at Columbia, which she’s done on the sly, surely she might have found academic success regionally, which would at least slightly soften the impact of her leaving. This geographical rigidity feels more like a dramatist’s shortcut than logical reality.

Other things also break the suspension of disbelief, like the moment, late in the show, when Ana and her shy boyfriend, Henry (Mason Reeves), engage in a halting, adolescent attempt at sex. The scene plays out with such exaggerated innocence that it borders on cartoonish. Given the time and setting—not to mention Ana’s intelligence and independence—their complete lack of sexual knowledge feels implausible. The scene adds nothing but time to the show, which clocks in at around two hours and 20 minutes, with one intermission,

Working with a score by Joy Huerta (music) and Huerta and Benjamin Velez (lyrics), director-choreographer Sergio Trujillo does his best to help the company express pleasingly melodic songs mixing Latin pop influences with traditional musical theatre stylings, although the results often sound more pastiche than unique. Songs like “If I Were a Bird” and “Daydream” aim for emotional resonance, but words and music feel generic. Numbers often reiterate plot points rather than reveal deeper character truths or move the action forward.

As a director, however, Trujillo never succeeds in finding the proper tone in a talky script that mingles sitcom and kitchen sink drama, as the audience patiently awaits the next musical number. His choreography, however, brings flair to several ensemble numbers, like “Make It Work,” “Adios Andres” (a paean to menopause), and “Real Women Have Curves,” the highlight. It requires that, because of the heat, the seamstresses, largely of sizable proportions, strip down to their skivvies, as the crowd roars. It’s meant to empower the women by having them shed their body-size concerns along with their clothes. It had the opposite effect on me, but many rose to applaud it. 

Compared to most of the other musicals this season, Real Women . . . is visually on the dull side. The subject matter, much of it transpiring in such dreary places as a sweatshop factory, a working-class kitchen, and a poor boy’s bedroom, isn’t the kind to inspire musical comedy glitz. Arnolfo Maldonado, aided by the warm lighting of Natasha Katz, does what he can to enliven the mostly static, muted environment, but his prettiest contribution is the Latin-inspired show curtain and proscenium décor. And Hana S. Kim’s projections indicating time and place offer little one remembers.

Wilberth Gonzalez and Paloma Young’s everyday costumes for the low-income characters face similar problems. They do get some relief in a lovely scene when dresses descend from the flies in a cascade of colors, and when the glammed-up garment workers step out in such colorful gowns during the finale. 

Tatianna Córdoba, in her Broadway debut (she holds a BFA from Boston Conservatory), as Ana, has a strong voice and a warm stage presence; when she dances with Henry, she’s gracefully supple. Justina Machado (TV’s One Day at a Time) has some fiery moments, but she’s stuck in a role that too often lacks credibility. Likewise, the supporting cast is appealing despite thinly drawn characters who seem more pasteboard than flesh.

Real Women Have Curves has its heart in the right place. Its desire to spotlight Latina stories, women’s solidarity, and working-class realities is important. But too much seems artificial and too little honest and truthful. It projects contrivance more than complexity, cliché more than originality, shallowness more than depth. Much of this is capsulized in a climactically melodramatic device when Mrs. Wright threatens not to pay for the dresses and Ana—thanks to her reporter’s job—saves the day. Fun, yes, but an old-fashioned solution.

Real Women Have Curves: The Musical is not a great fit. It’s held together by creative basting stitches, and frequently threatens to come apart at the seams.

Real Women Have Curves **1/2
James Earl Jones Theater, 138 W. 48th St., NYC.
Running time: two hours and 20 mins. including intermission. realwomenhavecurvesbroadway.com
April 27, 2025 — open run.

By Paulanne Simmons

May 2, 2025. Abby Stein was born Srully Abraham Stein to a Hassidic family living in Williamsburg, Brooklyn. She grew up speaking Yiddish and Hebrew. She attended an all-boys Jewish day school. But Abby felt profoundly uncomfortable with her gender and her community.  In 2012 she came out as an atheist. Later she came out as trans. In 2019 her memoir, Becoming Eve: My Journey from Ultra-Orthodox to Transgender Woman was published and became a bestseller.

Now her story has become a play, Becoming Eve, written by Emil Weinstein, directed by Tyne Rafaeli and staring Tommy Dorfman as Chava, the transgender woman who is desperately trying to get her father (the excellent Richard Schiff) to understand and accept her. The play opens with Chava and Jonah, her rabbi (Brandon Uranowitz), planning their strategy, which entails using scripture and Talmud to prove that a person can have a soul of a different gender.

After perhaps too much discussion, her father finally comes to Jonah‘s small office/sanctuary  (scenic designer Arnulfo Maldonado). It takes Chava, and the play a long time before Chava finally tells her father that she’s trans. This is partly because she finds it so difficult to face his wrath and disappointment, but also because the play veers back and forth between the present and the past.

We see Chava from birth through her childhood and adolescence to her marriage and divorce. Her mother (Judy Kuhn, remarkably underused for such a tremendous actor) is clueless but loving. Her friend and fellow-student, Chesky (Rad Pereira), provides comfort to the troubled adolescent. Her wife, Fraidy (Tedra Millan doing a great job in a difficult role), is remarkably understanding.

In these flashbacks, Chava is portrayed by different puppets reflecting her age, but Dorfman stands by to speak the puppet’s lines and sometimes enter into the action. Although the puppetry is excellent (the puppets were designed by Amanda Villalobos and are manipulated by Emma Wiseman and Justin Otaki Perkins), and they are an apt representation of how Chava felt she was being controlled by others and could never be herself, the stage does seem quite crowded.

Despite the serious subject, Becoming Eve has many truly funny moments, much of them supplied by Schiff, who shows a wonderful understanding of Jewish humor. Schiff also understands how love, disgust, anger and disappointment can all exist simultaneously. Dorfman is better in the flashbacks than in the scenes in the rabbi’s office, where she plays only one emotion, fear, except for one moment when she lashes out against her father.

Becoming Eve could easily lose a half hour. The long analyses of Hebrew text are unnecessary to the play and taxing to the audience. But even with its flaws, the play provides meaningful insight into a subject that for many is both painful and puzzling.

Becoming Eve ****
New York Theater Workshop at the Abrons Arts Center, 466 Grand St., NYC.
Running time: one hour and 50 mins. no intermission. nytw.org

By Samuel L. Leiter

May 1, 2025. As its new title suggests, the Roundabout Theatre Company’s sparkling, New Orleans jazz-inspired revival of Gilbert and Sullivan’s 1879 comic opera, The Pirates of Penzance; or, The Slave of Duty, has its satirical tongue firmly planted in its cheek, along with innumerable bits of musical and comic mischief. Regarding musical theater, it provides yet another reason to remember the 2024-2025 Broadway season as one of the brightest in years. 

Pirates! The Penzance Musical, now lighting up the Todd Haimes Theatre in a rendition hilariously adapted by Rupert Holmes (The Mystery of Edwin Drood), is scintillatingly directed by Scott Ellis (Take Me Out), and imaginatively choreographed by Warren Carlyle (Hello, Dolly!). It almost makes one forget the similarly radical version of 1980, starring Kevin Kline and Linda Ronstadt, that moved from Central Park to Broadway, and became the longest-running Gilbert and Sullivan production in history. If this nonprofit Roundabout Theatre production had an open run, it might even challenge that record.

The basic story, and its theme of duty in conflict with love, remain the same, of course: an orphaned lad named Frederic (Nicholas Barasch) has been indentured since birth to a band of softhearted, orphaned pirates, led by the Pirate King (Ramin Karimloo). (Orphan shtick is rampant, including a “Who’s on First”-like routine confusing “orphan” with “often.”)  He’s been raised by a woman named Ruth (Jinx Monsoon), the only woman he’s ever seen until he visits New Orleans and meets Mabel Stanley (Samantha Williams). When Frederic comes of age, at 21, and is no longer bound to the Pirate King, he learns that, since he was born in a leap year, he’s only five, and will have to wait until 1948 (in this version), when he’s in his 80s, to be free. This jape clashes with his romance with Mabel, who happens to be one of the multiple daughters of Major General Stanley (David Hyde Pearce). Naturally, his other girls become romantically entangled with the pirate crew, until all is happily unentangled at the end.

This Roundabout Theatre Company production shifts the silly tale from England to colorful, 19th-century New Orleans, seasoning its music as a jazzy jambalaya sauce of various cultural spices, sprinkling the dish with nonstop energy and laughter. It’s Gilbert and Sullivan as you’ve never heard it, with the blessings, in fact of that matchless pair themselves, who, dressed formally in tails, introduce the show in the persons of David Hyde Pearce (Gilbert) and Preston Truman Boyd (Sullivan), 

Pearce (Vanya and Sonia and Masha and Spike)makes a marvelously memorable mutton-chopped Major General, carrying his role with dry, unforced, deadpan humor. He delivers the show’s most famous patter song, the tongue-twisting “I Am the Very Model of a Modern Major General,” with tour-de-force technical perfection, even when the tempo increases to bullet train speed. 

Ramin Karimloo (Les Miserables) is insistently charismatic and athletic, displaying a powerhouse voice, superb dance chops, and deliciously aware, parodistic humor as the Pirate King. Costumed to show off his buff pectorals, he makes as striking a visual impression as a musical one. Jinkx Monsoon, a drag artist of ineffable charm and talent, is equally notable as Ruth, investing the role with expert comic timing, amusingly killer mugging, and vocal authority. 

Boyd as the tapdancing Sergeant of Police gives yet another superlative performance, as does Williams as the beautiful Mabel, resembling, at first sight, a young Audra McDonald. The entire company of 20, most of the women as sisters, most of the men as both pirates and Keystone Kops-like policemen, are expertly cast, carrying out their extremely arduous duties with never-flagging enthusiasm.

Warren Carlyle’s choreography is consistently fresh and vibrant, often using parasols to dazzling effect; Rick Sordelet and Christian Kelly-Sordelet outdo themselves in staging a masterfully complex fight scene involving the whole company; and Joseph Joubert’s music direction, combined with Daryl Waters’s commendable orchestrations, keeps our ears buzzing with New Orleans rhythms and flair, bringing novelty to even the most familiar songs. You may, though, find yourself wondering when you hear it, did G&S write “Hail, Hail, the Gang’s All Here”? And aficionados will likely spot numbers interpolated from other shows by the masters.

Linda Cho’s costumes are both gorgeous and witty, especially her unique vision for dressing the sisters in bustles and jeans. David Rockwell’s sets, one outside a New Orleans theatre in the French Quarter, and another—resembling something from the Addams Family—outside a moonlit mansion, are lovely, especially as lit by Donald Holder. One moment, in particular, struck me, when, after a miniature pirate ship is seen crossing the watery background, it’s followed by the ship’s huge prow shoved on from the wings. Precisely the same effect, in fact, has long been used in a kabuki play called Shunkan.

Pirates! The Penzance Musical is not your grandparents’ Pirates of Penzance. It remains faithful enough to the original to satisfy those who love Gilbert and Sullivan but long for original takes on their classics. It has enough comical wisdom to satisfy audiences who want to laugh at something with a 21st sensibility and not at what made people laugh in the 1880s. Even with all the competition for awards in this musical-dominated season, I think Pirates!, which runs two hours plus an intermission,is deft enough to steal your heart. 

Pirates! The Penzance Musical *****
Roundabout Theater Company at the Todd Haimes Theater, 227 W. 42nd St., NYC.
Running time: two hours and 20 mins. including intermission. roundabouttheatre.org
April 24—July 27, 2025.

title.rendered: Stranger Things: The First Shadow *****, Real Women Have Curves ****, Becoming Eve ****

content.rendered:
By David Sheward

April 28, 2025. If you’ve been waiting for the must-see production of the Broadway season to justify plunking down your hard-earned bucks, wait no more. Stranger Things: The First Shadow, now at the Marquis after an Olivier-winning run in London, is the most spectacular, fun show on the Main Stem in many years and will scare the crap out of you. A working knowledge of the cult-status Netflix series upon which it is based is not necessary. The plot takes place before the streaming TV show begins and Kate Trefry’s intricate script stands on its own. (The original story is credited to Trefry, a writer and co-executive producer for the series; the Duffer Brothers who created the show and directed many of its episodes; and Jack Thorne, author of Harry Potter and the Cursed Child, another London and Broadway smash based on a successful fantasy/sci-fi franchise.) 

Stephen Daldry and his co-director Justin Martin have staged the complex, absorbing story like a film with smoothly flowing scenes imparting vital information and thrills. But the real stars are the other-worldly special effects and illusions created by Jamie Harrison and Chris Fisher, which rival anything you’ll see on Broadway including a horrifying invasion from another dimension. My theatergoing companion called this specific effect the new and better chandelier from Phantom of the Opera or the helicopter from Miss Saigon. I’m not going to list themore nerve-rattling and spine-shaking moments so as not to spoil your fun, but suffice it to say, look out for crashing battleships, monsters with no faces, and be prepared to scream if you’re afraid of spiders.

Loyal viewers of the show will recognize the basic narrative template. (Full disclosure: in preparation for reviewing Stranger Things, I attempted to binge the series in a few weeks, but I only got through the first two seasons and half of the third.) The seemingly humdrum little town of Hawkins, Indiana is beset with weird occurrences. In the series, it started with the disappearance of a young boy. In the play, pets turn up dead. Gradually, we discover that a dark, ominous parallel universe is bleeding into the bucolic hamlet and a newly arrived, introverted teen holds the key to the mystery. The series commences in Reagan’s 1980s America and, in each season, whatever calamity rises up is defeated by a gang of plucky, outsider adolescents with a few token grown-ups helping out. The play skips back a generation to 1959 and the familiar adults are now the adventurous teens. Both timelines are dominated by the menacing Dr. Brenner who heads a shadowy Deep State lab which is mixed up in every cuckoo conspiracy besetting Hawkins.

The basic appeal of the series is the heroic status of the nerdy kids saving the day. The message is it’s okay to be considered weird, love science, and get good grades. The play emphasizes the painful struggles of the alienated youngsters at the center of the story. The amazing Louis McCartney repeats his London role as Henry Creel, the socially awkward loner somehow tied in with all the mysterious happenings. McCartney delivers a viscerally dynamic and shockingly physical performance as dark forces battle for Henry’s soul. Gabrielle Nevaeh is sensitive and intense as Patty Newby, the orphaned girl “from nowhere” who befriends Henry. 

The major problem I have with Trefry’s otherwise clever script is that it ignores the elephant in the room. Patty is cast as an African-American young woman adopted by a white family, headed by the conservative high school principal no less. In 1959 Indiana, this situation would not be glossed over. The only acknowledgment here is when Patty says she bears a resemble to Ella Fitzgerald. An accurate depiction of the racism of the period might have distracted from the main story, but it would have lent a note of bitter realism and added tension.

Alison Jaye, Burke Swenson, and understudy Patrick Scott McDermott (covering for Juan Carlos at the performance attended) are energetic as the amateur young sleuths who grow up to become the parents in the series. Eric Wiegand is a riot as an obsessed theater kid. Alex Breux is all ice and steel as the dangerous Dr. Brenner. T.R. Knight and Rosie Benton shutter and shatter admirably as Henry’s troubled parents. Andrew Hovelson and Ted Koch are pompously proper as other clueless grownups. 

Daldry and Martin’s fluid and dynamic direction is abetted by the magical, moving sets of Miriam Buether, the scary, atmospheric lighting of Jon Clark, the spooky and penetrating sound design of Paul Arditti, and the grainy, gritty videos of 59 Productions. D.J. Wade composed the haunted and haunting original music and Brigitte Riffenstuel deserves kudos for the period costumes.

There are plenty of scary moments in Stranger Things, but the new musical Real Women Have Curves has a horrifying sequence which is even more frightening because it’s really  happening across the country. Like Stranger Things, the setting is the 1980s. We are in a dress factory in Boyle Heights, Los Angeles. The ladies are hard at work on a rush order of 200 dresses which could make their brand. They hear a crash at the pillow factory next door. “Immigration!,” cries the boss Estela. She douses the lights and everyone hides under their sewing machines. There is silence for several terrifying seconds. The workers gradually emerge and resume their labors.

This scary scene in an otherwise joyful musical brings home the insecure status of undocumented aliens which persists some 40 years later. But the focus of this exuberant show is the strong bond among immigrant families and their struggles to get ahead. Based on Josefina Lopez’s play and the subsequent HBO film with a screenplay by Lopez and George LaVoo, Real Women celebrates the bond between sisters Estela and Ana and their determined mother Carmen. 

Estela labors intensely to make the dress factory a success while Ana, a budding journalist, has just received a full scholarship to attend Columbia University. But Carmen opposes Ana leaving the family when they need her the most to complete the rush order. In addition, Ana is the only citizen in the family and can therefore deal with government bureaucracy. The book by Lisa Loomer with Nell Benjamin leans a bit heavily on sentimental melodrama, but balances these soapy suds with sharp wit and a strong depiction of characters too often ignored in Broadway musicals. At one Carmen observes, “I’m 51 and I’ve working since I was 13. In gringa years, I’d be 70.”

The score by Joy Huerta and Benjamin Velez is equally snappy and irreverent as well as uplifting. The title song in which the factory ladies and Ana defy society’s body shaming and celebrate their ample shapes, brings the house down with its unapologetic defiance. In another group number tackling a subject you seldom hear about on Broadway, Carmen and the ladies welcome the onset of menopause and the exiting of their “monthly visitor.” There’s also soaring hopeful song for Ana and Itzel, a recent arrival from Guatemala, and a funny comedy number where Ana and her new boyfriend Henry attempt their first time at sex, but have no idea what to do. Sergio Trujillo skillfully directs and choreographs, combining biting humor with savvy movement. Arnulfo Maldonado’s sets create a believable LA atmosphere, along with Hana S. Kim’s videos and Natasha Katz’s lighting. WIlberth Ganzalez and Paloma Young’s costumes blend the everyday life of the workers with their high-fashion aspirations.

Tatiana Cordoba, Florencia Cuenca, and Justina Machado are fierce, funny, and fiery as Ana, Estela, and Carmen, as are Mason Reeves as Henry and Aline Mayagoitia as Itzel. Real Women is the real thing, a Broadway show with heart and courage addressing marginalized people. 

Speaking of real women and underrepresented populations, the modern world of fluid sexuality clashes with the rigid rules of Jewish orthodoxy in Becoming Eve, Emil Weinstein’s powerful and thought-provoking stage adaptation of Abby Chava Stein’s memoir. Presented by New York Theater Workshop at the Abrons Arts Center (recently closed), the compassionate play switches narrative tracks between the present-day confrontation between Chava (Hebrew for Eve), a transgender woman and her traditionalist rabbi father (with facilitation by reform rabbi Jonah) and flashbacks to Eve’s past. Chava has not revealed her transition from man to woman to her dad and seeks to soften to blow by citing Talmudic scripture. With the aide of Jonah, Chava has prepared examples from the story of Abraham and Isaac, referencing a scholar’s interpretation that Isaac had a female soul and was transformed to a male when Abraham was called to sacrifice his life by God. 

In the flashbacks, Chava is embodied by elaborate puppets designed by Amanda Villalobos while her voice is provided by the actor playing the role, an expressive Tommy Dorfman, suggesting that her former self was not her true being. Tyne Rafaeli’s direction carefully balances the forceful debate with the conflicting emotions of each of the parties. Dorfman’s tormented but ultimately triumphant Chava, Richard Schiff’s rigid but intellectual father, and Brandon Uranowitz’s amicable Jonah give depth to each corner of this dramatic triangle.

By David Sheward

April 28, 2025. If you’ve been waiting for the must-see production of the Broadway season to justify plunking down your hard-earned bucks, wait no more. Stranger Things: The First Shadow, now at the Marquis after an Olivier-winning run in London, is the most spectacular, fun show on the Main Stem in many years and will scare the crap out of you. A working knowledge of the cult-status Netflix series upon which it is based is not necessary. The plot takes place before the streaming TV show begins and Kate Trefry’s intricate script stands on its own. (The original story is credited to Trefry, a writer and co-executive producer for the series; the Duffer Brothers who created the show and directed many of its episodes; and Jack Thorne, author of Harry Potter and the Cursed Child, another London and Broadway smash based on a successful fantasy/sci-fi franchise.)

content.rendered:
By Samuel L. Leiter

April 27, 2025. Before seeing Broadway’s Stranger Things: The First Shadow, originally produced on London’s West End in 2023, and now at the Marquis Theatre, I thought I’d binge on the hit Netflix series for which its story is the prequel. I began with the first episode of its four-season run (a fifth is in the works), but halfway through realized I’d already seen a few episodes years ago. And that was all I’d seen. I now made it through only the first two episodes, which, obviously, deprived me of anything like the fan adulation, even exaltation, and inside knowledge shared by so many in the youth-oriented audience who are visiting it in droves. The expansive Marquis, fortunately, is a perfect venue for a show whose remarkable special effects serve a melodramatic, but increasingly chaotic plot about eerie, supernatural happenings in a small Midwestern town. 

It reminded me of the spectacular melodramas of the Victorian age, when audiences were anxious to witness heroes survive and villains foiled in plots involving stage-shuddering explosions and natural catastrophes. These were represented by exciting scenic breakthroughs that seem like child’s play when compared to what’s available today. Stranger Things: The First Shadow is a showcase for what’s possible if you have over $50 million to spend on state-of-the-art projections, scenic technology, eyepopping lighting, computerized gimmicks, a revolving stage, and a cast of over 30 dressed in the clothing of the late 1950s.

For the record: Miriam Buether did the sets, Jon Clark the lighting, Brigitte Rieffenstuel the costumes, Paul Arditty the sound, Jamie Harrison and Chris Fisher the illusions and visual effects, and 59 the video and visual effects (the distinctions between the last two credits are beyond my ken).

Monstrous creatures tower, people elevate, characters appear simultaneously in duplicate, a gigantic naval ship founders, a car floats, sparks shower, lightning flashes, spider legs pop out of a boy’s body, and unworldly sounds overwhelm, as the jaw-dropping effects keep topping themselves, often startlingly. Every penny of it shows.

Soon after the show begins, we’re gobsmacked with an unforgettably fiery scene—during which clouds of smoke engulf the theatre—involving an American naval ship involved in a secret military experiment in 1943, one that takes us to another dimension that seeds what will appear some years later. 

The action moves to Hawkins, Indiana, in 1959, 27 years before 1986, when the TV series takes place. We now meet the central character, a weird, twitchily high-strung teen named Henry Creel (the excellent Irish newcomer, Louis McCartney, the sole actor from the London production). Possessed of dangerous psychokinetic powers linked to that 1943 experiment, he will become the monstrous Vecna on the TV series. Henry, his little sister, Alice (Azalea Wolfe at the performance I attended), and parents, Virginia (Rose Benton) and Victor (T.R. Knight), have moved here from Nevada, but Henry has trouble fitting in with the local teens. These include younger versions of the characters fans are familiar with from the TV series, among them future police officer Jim Hopper, Jr. (Burke Swanson), theatre geek Joyce Maldonado (Alison Jaye), and Bob Newby (Juan Carlos).

Henry befriends Patty Newby (Gabrielle Nevaeh), burdened by her own issues (her uptight dad is the principal), and is cast opposite her as the witch boy in a student production of Dark of the Moon. It’s directed by the hyper-charged Joyce, who has chosen it instead of the expected Oklahoma! 

Snippets of that show’s music are, in fact, sung by enthusiastic students. Moreover, recorded bits of several standards (“Dream a Little Dream of Me,” “Have Yourself a Merry Little Christmas,” etc.) are interpolated throughout the script, most extensively “The Nearness of You,” suggesting just how close Stranger Things is to becoming a musical. There’s so much choreographed stage movement, you often expect the actors to break into dance, which indeed happens once or twice. (Movement director and choreographer: Lynne Page; additional choreography: Corral Messam.)

Henry gradually descends into darkness as a monstrous being inside him begins to emerge. A succession of local cats is viciously slain, and Henry loses his mother and sister. He becomes the unwilling subject of intense examination by a scientist named Dr. Brenner (Alex Breaux), seeking to harness his powers. Various forms of mayhem ensue. 

I was particularly interested in the inclusion of Dark of the Moon (not, as the dialogue has it, THE Dark of the Moon) because, in 1945, it was the first Broadway play my parents ever took me to; I even directed a college production of this backwoods play inspired by the legend of Barbara Allen in the mid-1980s. Its story of a boy with magical powers—which Henry has in abundance—has obvious relevance for the world of Stranger Things. If only the new play shared the poetic depth of Dark of the Moon it might have made as much of a dramatic impression as the wizardry of its production.

Stephen Daldry and codirector Justin Martin keep the performance on a larger-than-life, almost operatic scale, comparable to that of the visual exaggeration. This forces the play—by series writer Kate Trefry, with contributions from the series creators Duffer Brothers and Jack Thorne (who wrote the far superior Harry Potter and the Cursed Child)—to depend on characters who shout more than they speak, run rather than walk, and speed like demons through a plot whose already challenged credibility becomes increasingly muddled, sometimes leaving Stranger Things duffers like me on the dark side of the moon. 

Everyone gives it the old college—high school, I mean—try and without their boundless eagerness the unnecessarily long (nearly three-hours) show would flounder even more. Most visitors obviously relish the excess, but others, like me, may find the relentless pace, noise, and succession of effects growing wearisome, replacing suspense about what’s going to happen next with suspense about when it’s going to end. 

While duly impressed by the technical innovations, I was unimpressed by the drama, much like my reaction to Julie Taymor’s equally spectacular, zillion-dollar production of Spiderman: Turn Off the Dark. Unlike that disaster, though, the general response to Stranger Things: The First Shadow suggests it will be haunting Broadway for some time to come. And, given its brand name, and how that’s being marketed in the Marquis lobby, the money should flow copiously from both stage and merch.

By Paulanne Simmons

April 25, 2025. In recent years, Broadway audiences have seen several reinterpretations of classic musicals. But no one has reinvented a classic with the perfect mix of innovation and fidelity to the spirit of the original material like the creators of Pirates! the Penzance Musical.

Adaptor Rupert Holmes (The Mystery of Edwin Drood, Curtains) has set the story in New Orleans (once a hub for pirates, who used the bayous and swamps of the gulf coast for smuggling). And orchestrator Joseph Joubert (also musical director)andDaryl Waters have given Arthur Sullivan’s music a jaunty, bluesy Caribbean beat.

Some of W. S. Gilbert’s dialogue and lyrics have been changed. But David Hyde Pierce, who plays Major General Stanley (as well as William S. Gilbert), sings the crowd-pleasing, tongue-twisting “I Am the Very Model of a Modern Major-General” with all the original ridiculous British priggishness Gilbert and Sullivan intended.

The show, directed by Scott Ellis, is a rollicking good time, from the first moment William S. Gilbert and Arthur Sullivan (Preston Truman Bond) walk onstage to inform the audience that the show is making its premiere in New Orleans to avoid copyright infringement (something that often happened to Gilbert and Sullivan operettas in the United States), to the last scene when we are reminded that the United States is a nation of immigrants.

Nicholas Barasch is a talented tenor who plays Frederic, the unfortunate “slave of duty,” who has been mistakenly indentured to a band of pirates, with comic sincerity. The hardworking Ramin Karimloo who is Frederic’s sometimes friend, sometimes foe, the Pirate King, jumps onto barrels, brandishes his sword and belts his songs with great vigor.

The comic role of Ruth, the befuddled and besotted nurse, who has taken care of Frederic since he was a baby, shines in the hands of Jinkx Monsoon, a two-time winner of RuPaul’s Drag Race. Her bawdy femininity is in sharp contrast to the coy but hilarious reserve of the Major-General’s daughters, especially Mabel (Samantha Williams), who captures Frederic’s heart. 

With all those sword-swinging pirates, and fluttering maidens, this Gilbert and Sullivan operetta is choreographer’s dream, and Warren Carlyle has dreamed up some wonderful choreography. The dancers prance their way through a whimsical, sometimes impressionistic set colorfully created by David Rockwell.

Pirates! The Penzance Musical borrows from both HMS Pinafore (the first act closer “The ‘Sail the Ocean’ Blues”) and The Mikado (“Alone and Yet Alive”). This is entirely in keeping with Gilbert and Sullivan’s often self-referential comedy. After all, even in the original they have the Major-General sing “And whistle all the airs/from that infernal nonsense Pinafore.”

In fact, we can be pretty sure if Gilbert and Sullivan could only see this irreverent but sound revival they’d say, “Jolly good show!”

content.rendered:
By David Sheward

April 24, 2025. The beloved, whimsical operettas of W.S. Gilbert and Arthur Sullivan, composed between 1871 and 1896, have had their share of updating and transpositions. There has been a Hot Mikado and a Swing Mikado in 1939 and a Hollywood Pinafore in 1945. So it should come as no surprise that there would eventually be a reworking of one of G&S’s most popular pieces, The Pirates of Penzance, particularly after Wilford Leach’s smash hit revival played Central Park in 1980 and then transferred to Broadway in ’81. For Roundabout Theater Company, Rupert Holmes (The Mystery of Edwin Drood) has changed the setting from the British coast to New Orleans, cut a few numbers, added others from the G&S canon, rewritten some of Gilbert’s book and lyrics, jazzed up Sullivan’s score, and we now have Pirates! The Penzance Musical. Never mind that the title doesn’t make any sense because all references to Penzance, a seaside town in Cornwall, have been excised. This is a delightful reworking which is not an improvement on the original, but just as much fun.

Holmes’ premise is that Gilbert and Sullivan (played by David Hyde-Pierce and Preston Truman Boyd in a prologue) are presenting the American premiere of their latest work in the Big Easy because the area has such a rich history of piracy. Plus they want to establish a Yankee copyright and avoid the numerous pirated productions (get it?) of their previous big hit HMS Pinafore. (For the record, Pirates actually debuted in NYC for the latter reason in 1879.) What follows is a spicy musical jumbo with orchestrators Joseph Joubert and Daryl Waters mixing Dixieland, the blues, jazz and r&b with G&S’s frothy original recipe (Joubert also capably serves as musical director.) Holmes’ new book sometimes condescends to the audience, explaining Gilbert’s wordplay and simplifying his lyrics here and there. 

Holmes does get a bit heavy-handed with the modern references. Major-General Stanley’s flighty daughters now sing of their quest for suffrage, and the pirates finally surrender, not out of loyalty to Queen Victoria as in the original, but after an appeal to unity in American diversity. The final number is a variation on “He Is an Englishman” from Pinafore. Rather than jingoistically praising the glories of England (“In spite of all temptations/To belong to other nations”), the chorus now harmonizes on a paen to the immigrant experience with “We all come from someplace else.”

However, these are minor caveats. Director Scott Ellis and choreographer Warren Carlyle have infused the proceedings with zany zest. The famous  “I Am the Model of a Modern Major-General,” delightfully and drily delivered by Hyde Pierce, is accompanied by the chorus madly waving signal flags. The first act concludes with everyone strumming washboards and ringing bells. The finale and curtain call are followed by cast members sashaying up the aisles, flinging beads as they go.

As noted, Hyde Pierce is a deadpan delight as the marvelously muddled Major-General. In addition to the traditional tongue-twisting solo, he is given “The Nightmare Song” from Iolanthe, elaborately staged by Ellis and Carlyle. Hyde Pierce and the chorus act out each of Stanley’s bizarre dreams, make this a riotous descend into lunacy. Ramin Karimloo is swoon-worthy, virile Pirate King. Jinkx Monsoon (RuPaul’s Drag Race) is a riotous Ruth and delivers a surprisingly heartfelt and bluesy “Alone and Yet Alive,” Katisha’s lament from The Mikado. Nicholas Barasch and Samantha Williams display admirable pipes and gleefully satirize young-lovers tropes as the main amorous duo, Frederick and Mabel. Boyd doubles as the scaredy-cat Sergeant, hilariously shivering as he leads a quivering platoon of police against the pirates. 

Throw in David Rockwell’s cartoonish sets, Linda Cho’s eccentric costumes, and Donald Holder’s painterly lighting and this Pirates! is a jolly good time.

content.rendered:
By David Sheward

April 22, 2025. Two dramas on teen torment recently opened on and Off-Broadway, approaching their subjects through different lenses and both achieving dynamic theatrical results. Kimberly Belflower’s John Proctor Is the Villain at the Booth offers a radical reinterpretation of Arthur Miller’s The Crucible as its starting point, but the play itself is rather conventionally structured. Off-Broadway at the Atlantic Theater Company, Eliya Smith’s Grief Camp takes what could have a Lifetime TV-movie plot—teens at camp dealing with the deaths of loved ones—and gives it an unconventional twist. Her play is a disturbing, puzzling, yet ultimately satisfying portrait of adolescent angst, as is Belflower’s work.

Set in 2018 at the height of the #MeToo movement, in a one-stoplight Georgia town, John Proctor follows the treacherous and tricky path trod by a group of high-school students as they study Miller’s classic play on the Salem witch trials and find parallels to their own situation. The girls in Mr. Smith’s Honors English class are wrestling with their burgeoning sexuality and an atmosphere of male repression. When they form a feminism club, it raises hackles in the conservative town as accusations of adult misconduct surface. Ivy’s dad has allegedly committed harassment with more than one woman, Raelynn is being pressured by her boyfriend Lee to have sex, and Shelby is returning to school after a mysterious absence. Shelby emerges as the main character as the shocking reason for her “sabbatical,” as she calls it, is revealed and she challenges the standard interpretation of John Proctor as the hero of The Crucible and his accuser Abigail as the villainess.   

Additional plot strands involve straight-A student Beth whose faith in her favorite teacher Mr. Smith is severely tested; new counselor Ms. Gallagher, barely older than the kids, attempting to make her mark; recent Atlanta transplant Nell navigating her way through treacherous waters; and Mason, trying his best to be a male ally.

Belflower captures the roiling ambivalent emotions of the students and teachers, combining raucous humor with raw pathos. Danya Taymor’s direction is fast-paced and pulsing with tension just beneath the day-to-day schoolroom surface. Sadie Sink (Stranger Things, The Whale) has a dynamic, captivating, jittery energy as Shelby. She covers her secret vulnerability with a rush of snarky observations, and gradually peels back Shelby’s tough exterior to reveal a shaky, confused kid. Amalia Yoo’s questioning Raelynn and Maggie Kuntz’s rattled Ivy are movingly insecure. Morgan Scott as Nell has several funny moments as does Fina Strazza as the overeager Beth. Hagan Oliveras and Nihar Duvvuri make the boys Lee and Mason more than adolescent stereotypes. Gabriel Ebert displays layers of deceit as the seemingly model teacher Mr. Smith and Molly Griggs shows Ms. Gallagher’s hidden strength.

Natasha Katz’s supernatural, spooky lighting transforms the detailed classroom set by AMP Ft. and Teresa L. Williams into a frightening nightmarescape.  

It’s especially refreshing to see a play by a new playwright on Broadway, but also to see new audiences. At the performance attended, there were numerous school groups and younger patrons. I can’t tell you the number of times I’ve been to a Broadway show and I was the youngest one there—and I’m in my 60s.

You don’t need to brush up on your Arthur Miller or the song catalogues of the latest pop stars to fully enjoy the jolting John Proctor, but it couldn’t hurt. 

Meanwhile, Off-Broadway, Eliya Smith’s Grief Camp takes a look at a similarly confused bunch of kids, but her portraiture is more fragmentary, messy and intriguing than Belflower’s. We first meet the campers in a stereotypical moment, talking after lights out. But it’s gradually revealed this is no ordinary camp, each of the teens has suffered the recent loss of a family member and they are here to heal. 

Each is dealing with mourning in peculiarly individual ways. Olivia (Renee-Nicole Powell) shamelessly flirts with her older counselor Cade (Jack DiFalco), explicitly bringing up menstruation and masturbation. Olivia’s sister Esther (Lark White) concentrates on becoming the most beautiful person in the world and her friend Luna (Grace Brennan) pretends to be from California, when she’s really from the Midwest. The shy Blue (Maaike Laanstra-Corn) is writing an elaborate musical fantasy involving a woman in a castle who converses with the ocean. Bard (Arjun Athalye) clings to his childhood sleep toy, a stuffed dinosaur, but finally resolves to throw it in the lake after it has been ripped open by the other kids. Gideon (Dominic Gross) is the one character woefully underdeveloped. Even Rocky (Danny Wolohan) the head counselor who we only know about through his rambling announcements over the P.A. system, is a deeper presence.

In addition to Gideon’s slight characterization, there were some flaws. Would teenage boys and girls be sharing the same cabin and toilet facilities? (Louisa Thompson designed the appropriately rustic set.) An adult onstage guitarist (Alden Harris-McCoy) provides occasional musical accompaniment and interacts with Bard in one fishing scene, but it’s not clear what his role is. Is he a counselor or a device of the playwright? The setting of Hurt, Virginia is little too on the nose. But despite these problems, Smith has created a quirky, arresting portrait of kids dealing with life-crushing circumstances, directed with sensitivity by Les Waters and acted with depth by a surprisingly insightful young cast. I was particularly fascinated by Powell’s bitchy, yet vulnerable Olivia and Laanstra-Corn’s  off-kilter Blue. In the play’s final moment, she tearfully sings a song from her bizarre script and then becomes an older version of herself, counseling a suffering camper, and reliving the stages of her own grief. It’s a beautiful moment in an imperfect, strange play I won’t soon forget.

content.rendered:
By Samuel L. Leiter

April 22, 2025. Two current plays, one on Broadway and one Off, seem designed to attract younger audiences with their granular depiction of teenage angst, lingo, and behavior. Both have serious purposes, mingling dark emotion with dashes of laughter to offer insight into the hormonally active psyches of high school kids. The one on Broadway, Kimberly Belflower’s John Proctor Is the Villain, is by far the superior, with its fully developed characters, dramatic arc, and ideational subtext. The other, Grief Camp, by Eliya Smith (making her Off-Broadway debut), is decently directed at the Atlantic by Les Waters, but it’s dramatically flat and emotionally uninvolving.

As the title notes, it’s set at a grief camp (some call them bereavement camps), a summer camp where the guests are provided with services to help them cope with recent traumatic losses, typically the death of a parent or sibling. The camp we see in Smith’s play is, in most respects, like traditional ones, although I was surprised to see that the six campers we meet, two boys and four girls, all bunk in the same large room, realistically designed by Louisa Thompson, with a porch running upstage along its audience left side. The door to the one bathroom is up center. It’s nicely lit by Isabella Byrd and effectively costumed in typical teen grunge by Oana Botez. 

The camp is located on property owned and operated by someone named Rocky (Danny Wolohan), whom we never see but whose avuncular voice (and awful bugle renditions of “Reveille”) we hear every morning over the scratchy PA system. It offers all the typical activities one would expect, like riding, fishing, and swimming, evening movies, firefly chasing, card playing, etc. 

However, all campers must perform “chores,” and engage in daily “one-on-one” counseling sessions. It’s not clear if there are other counselors (or even if there are other campers), but the one counselor we meet, Cade (Jack DiFalco), is a young man who sleeps in the same room with his charges. We can be forgiven for thinking he’s one of the campers until his real function is revealed.

We’re about one third into the play before the nature of the camp becomes clear; otherwise, we witness the day to day, moment to moment interactions of the campers, who, despite their individual quirks, rarely project any idea of the depths of their grief, or even of what caused their trauma. Only later in the play do we casually hear from two or three about such things. Meanwhile, there’s very little else to latch on to other than watching a group of mostly bored teenagers get through their daily routines. 

One eccentric girl, for example, Blue (Maaike Laanstra-Corn), is writing an odd, one-person musical to be presented by her at her school. Its lines—which she periodically recites—are filled with poetic, surrealistic images—the ocean figuring prominently; whatever subtextual meanings they may bear, they sound bafflingly pretentious when spoken. They also occupy more stage time than they deserve.

Another girl, Olivia (Renée-Nicole Powell), openly talks to Cade about her intimate issues (such as yeast infections and masturbation), and comes on strong, forcing the uncomfortable counselor to respond as tactfully as he can. He himself has obvious emotional issues—he has a degree in engineering but it seems of little value to him—but nothing much comes of them. Nor is much made of any specific camper’s traumatic experiences, or even of the value of what little therapy they engage in. During the one, abbreviated session shown, the camper, asked to respond to a question about guilt, has no interest in following through.

Aside from playing up the campers’ occasional personality tics, teenage anxieties, and various interchanges, Grief Camp simply meanders from one day to the next. Regardless of the potential for emotional stakes in the circumstances, the play leaves them largely unexplored. Perhaps the most theatrical moment comes when several campers stand downstage in drenching rain. Even the play’s brief 100-minute runtime can’t prevent the onset of ennui, not unlike what the restless kids on display might feel when the weather remains too damp or hot to have any fun.

There’s nothing wrong with the acting, which believably captures the youthful naivete, burgeoning sensitivities, and intelligence of these articulate, presumably upper middle-class kids. Their language, while not as pitch-perfectly natural as that of the students in John Proctor Is the Villain, is sufficiently convincing, although Smith sometimes throws in a puzzler that fails the plausibility test. At one point, for instance, a boy named Gideon (Dominic Gross) declares, in response to another camper, Bard (Arjun Athalye), who wants his name pronounced Brad: “I want my delivery to connote the hollowness of inauthenticity, while celebrating your right to self-identity.” Who speaks like that?

Playwrights have to start somewhere, and Eliya Smith is fortunate to be able to kick off her Off-Broadway presence with a polished mounting at the Atlantic. For that alone, regardless of her play’s fate, she should have little about which to grieve.

Grief Camp **1/2

April 22, 2025. Two current plays, one on Broadway and one Off, seem designed to attract younger audiences with their granular depiction of teenage angst, lingo, and behavior. Both have serious purposes, mingling dark emotion with dashes of laughter to offer insight into the hormonally active psyches of high school kids. The one on Broadway, Kimberly Belflower’s John Proctor Is the Villain,is by far the superior, with its fully developed characters, dramatic arc, and ideational subtext. The other, Grief Camp, by Eliya Smith (making her Off-Broadway debut), is decently directed at the Atlantic by Les Waters, but it’s dramatically flat and emotionally uninvolving.

By Samuel L. Leiter

April 20, 2025. As we exited the Samuel J. Friedman Theatre after seeing Sondheim’s Old Friends, producer-devisor Cameron Mackintosh’s revue of around 40 songs by Stephen Sondheim, my companion and I agreed that experiencing the show was a rare privilege. Not only because of the opportunity to bask for two hours and 45 minutes in the words and music of the greatest Broadway songwriter since Rodgers and Hammerstein, but because it was presented, as if on a golden salver, by such a brilliant company of first-class singers, some of them first-class dancers as well. 

New York now has the privilege of experiencing the show, which began as a one-night London concert in 2022, premiered on the West End in 2023, and saw a production earlier this year at the Ahmanson Theatre Center in Los Angeles. 

Superstars Bernadette Peters and Lea Salonga starred in both the West End and L.A. productions, and now head a company of nearly 20, each of whom gives their own superstar-level performance, serving the material with consistently dazzling brilliance. With sparkling direction and musical staging by Matthew Bourne, and limited but expert choreography by Stephen Moore, Sondheim’s Old Friends is, from start to finish, a show that audiences will long remember.

Aside from some introductory words by Peters and Salonga penned by James Lapine, Sondheim’s Old Friends depends on the songs alone, without commentary, to carry the evening. One number follows the other, with the performers getting multiple opportunities to show their stuff. The first act is essentially, but not entirely, a series of capsule-sized introductions to Company, Into the Woods, A Little Night Music, and Sweeney Todd, each represented by two or more songs. But before that, the show opens with “Side by Side,” sung by the two leads, and the ensemble number, “Comedy Tonight,” from A Funny Thing Happened on the Way to the Forum.

The second act, while offering multiple numbers from selected shows, mixes them up a bit, so we get “Broadway Babies” from Follies followed by “Everybody Ought to Have a Maid” from A Funny Thing . . . , and then “You’ve Gotta Get a Gimmick” from Gypsy, before moving back to several songs from Follies, beginning with “Waiting for the Girls Upstairs.” 

Some songs appear just because they deserve inclusion, the time saved by not having spoken commentary providing that much more room to enjoy them. The biggest surprise may be “The Boy From . . . ,” a hilarious spoof of the bossa nova classic, “The Boy from Ipanema,” first heard in a 1966 revue called The Mad Show cowritten with Mary Rodgers. Delivered with hilarious panache by the stunningly sinuous, cocktail-sipping Kate Jennings Grant in a sleek, body-hugging sheath, its unfamiliarity—except for Sondheimaniacs—makes it (and her) stand out. 

Peters, looking from row M no different than she did God knows how many years ago, is unforgettable warbling such songs as “Children Will Listen” and, heartbreakingly, “Losing My Mind.” She also reminds us of her superpowers whenever she does a duet with Salonga, as in the title song, or even in her frequent ensemble routines. Ditto Salonga. There’s not a hint of star rivalry on display, the joy of singing Sondheim creating a unified esprit de corps. There’s plenty of space for others to demonstrate their remarkable talents, too many to cite, although I must say that, on a day when I dressed for the warm weather, Bonnie Langford’s “I’m Still Here” and Beth Leavel’s “The Ladies Who Lunch” were among the numbers that knocked my Crocs off.

As some will notice, the songs include not just those for which Sondheim wrote the music and lyrics, but two each from Gypsy and West Side Story, for which he wrote just the words. Thank goodness, or we wouldn’t have had the fun of hearing Bernadette Peters, doing Miss Mazeppa as a worn-out stripper, bump it with a trumpet, or Lea Salonga rivaling Audra McDonald’s clarion voice a couple of blocks away on “Everything’s Coming up Roses.”  

Matt Kinley’s clever scenery combines a neutral revue look—an upstage bandstand platform for the 17-member orchestra (led by Annbritt duChapeau) connected to open staircases at either side—with selective units slid on to suggest a particular show or two. Similarly, Jill Parker’s costumes go from nonspecific Broadway glamor to role-specific costumes and even wigs (by Stefan Musch), as when Salonga and the powerful Jeremy Secomb portray Mrs. Lovett and Sweeney in Sweeney Todd. Warren Letton’s lighting is perfect, and George Reeve’s projection design, including a show-ending video collage of Sondheim photos, helps greatly.

My sole cavil is that the program doesn’t identify the songs by the shows they come from. Otherwise, the genius of Sondheim’s Old Friends speaks for itself.

Stephen Sondheim’s Old Friends *****
Manhattan Theater Club at the Samuel J. Friedman Theater, 261 W. 47th St., NYC.

title.rendered: Five Reasons Why Operation Mincemeat Epitomizes Historical Humor

content.rendered:
By Iris Wiener

April 19, 2025. There’s nothing better than a musical that explores unchartered territory. Operation Mincemeat’s originality is startlingly refreshing, if scarily relevant. The borderline inconceivable story is centered during World War II, as the Allies were about to invade Sicily; a pair of British intelligence officers concocted the idea of deceiving the Nazis into believing the invasion would take place somewhere else. Why? Their hope was that the Nazis would deploy their troops elsewhere. The British officers went on to find a deceased homeless man, disguised him as an officer of the Royal Marines, planted fabricated documents that detailed the Allied battle plans, and dumped his body off the coast of Spain. Again, why? They hoped the Nazi spies would discover the made-up plans from the seemingly drowned man. The most bizarre aspect of this musical is that Operation Mincemeat was reality. The plan worked, and now serves as the plot of a must-see musical. Here are five reasons not to miss it:

1) Mincemeat’s intelligent book, written by comedy troupe SpitLip, manages to shed light on intricate details of this bizarre, unlikely experience, while making poignant connections to the current political climate. Though it has something of a Monty Python feel in its execution, it also has heart. See the song “Dear Bill,” in a ballad in which secretary Hester Leggett writes a fictional love letter to the fabricated dead officer to make his life more realized. Through a dynamic delivery from performer Jak Malone, the audience is gripped on a new level. Though there isn’t always tremendous action in the plot, there is always drive in the storytelling, with movement and smart segways between the uproarious numbers. 

2) The show is performed with precision and adept humor, an epic race of skill that one would be challenged to find anywhere else on Broadway. SpitLip members David Cumming, Natasha Hodgson, Zoe Roberts, along with Jak Malone and Claire-Marie Hall, are limitless in their energy and ability to transform into a multitude of roles. They swap genders, tones, and accents flawlessly within seconds, taking satirical parodies to new distinctly brilliant levels. 

3) The five actors switch roles and genders with lightning speed, giving a master class in quick changes and comedic accessibility. Ben Stones’ clever set, which at first seems simple, is in on the action, servicing the mania at all ends. His costumes are equally dynamic, and set the tone for clever use of the imagination. 

4) In addition to writing the book, SpitLips’ Cumming, Hodgson, Roberts, and Felix Hagan, penned the phenomenal multi-genre score and lyrics as well. Mincemeat could only be described as Six meets The Producers meets Hamilton. No two songs are alike, each poking at the truth in the story in different ways. (See the ballads, electronic dance numbers, vaudevillian acts, and sea shanties.) The actors are so luminous that they grip the audience in the palm of its hands. This team of sensational clowns are an epic gift to Broadway. 

5) New Yorkers will want to be in on the fun of the little show that could. Mincemeat began in a tiny 80-seat theatre way off the beaten path in the West End; it eventually became a West End hit, winning the Olivier Award for Best Musical. The show continues to be a massive success overseas, and is following suit on Broadway. Our prediction is that audiences will feel lucky to have been in the know come June, when the show begins to feel the American theatre awards accolades as well. 

    Operation Mincemeat ***
    The Golden Theatre, 252 W 45th St., NYC. 
    Running time: 2 hours, 35 mins. with 20 mins. intermission. operationbroadway.com
    Through August 18, 2025.
    Photography: Julieta Cervantes

title.rendered: Glass. Kill. What If If Only. Imp. ****, Wine in the Wilderness ****

content.rendered:
By David Sheward

April 19, 2025. You never know what you’re going to get with a Caryl Churchill play, but it’s sure to be something unique, thought-provoking, and convention-breaking. After exploring gender and racial barriers in Cloud 9, the clash of capitalism and feminism in Top Girls, financial turmoil in Serious Money, magic and demons in The Skirker, cloning in A Number, and numerous other topics in bizarre and weird ways, she tackles the power of legends, myths, and metaphor in a quartet of odd but affecting one-acts, Glass. Kill. What If If Only. Imp. at the Public Theater. 

The first three playlets are short and explosive, detonating like miniature bombs. Director James MacDonald has separated them with entertaining circus acts, performed with winning charm by balancing whiz Junru Wang and expert juggler Maddox Morfit-Tighe. These fun interludes act as palate cleansers between Churchill’s short unusual dramatic courses. Glass concerns a girl made of glass (played with appropriate delicacy and yearning by Ayana Workman). She is easily breakable and transparent, not just physically but emotionally. MacDonald stages the play on a narrow ledge, emphasizing the precarious space the girl occupies. There is no special costume or effect to convey her crystalline condition, MacDonald and Churchill ask us to use our imagination as she converses with the family clock, a ceramic dog and a vase on the need to remain still on a shelf. She falls for an equally vulnerable boy (tender Japhet Balaban), who is victimized by an abusive father. The climax of this bitter fairy tale is shattering, literally and figuratively. 

The powerful Deirdre O’Connell represents “Gods” in the following piece Kill, a Beckett-like monologue. Costume designer Enver Chakartash has clad her in a silvery suit with the suggestion of wings and she is seated on a suspended cloud. After stating that the gods do not exist, she launches on an epic retelling of the numerous tragedies surrounding the House of Atreus. Phrases detailing the murders within Agamemnon’s family and the endless slaughters that followed are repeated emphasizing the senseless of death in the name of the deities. (The repetitions and circular nature of the speech reminded me of Lucky’s monologue in Waiting for Godot.) O’Connell’s character is a symbol for the made-up supreme beings of mythologies used to explain humanity’s inhumanity. O’Connell delivers this tirade with a leavening of humor and growing passion which finally erupts in an explosion of anger at the useless killing.

What If If Only is the most esoteric and symbolic of the first three one-acts and has the least impact. A lonely widower (sensitive Saytha Sridharan) called simply Someone is mourning the loss of his young wife. Her ghost (Workman again) suddenly appears, but there is a catch. She brings with her phantoms representing all the unrealized futures that might have occurred had she lived. MacDonald cleverly solves this unusual stage problem. He has the walls of set designer Miriam Buether’s white cube of a living space lift up and the rest of the cast floods in overwhelming Someone. The ghosts including the wife flee, living only the Present (jovial John Ellison Conlee) and a child representing the unknown future (a self-assured Ruby Blaut at the performance attended.) Her only line, repeated a few times, is “I’m going to happen.” Despite MacDonald’s admirable staging, Churchill’s concept is too abstract to move us. The characters are all too generic for us to care about them. We can accept the concept of a girl made of glass because of the specific, detailed life Churchill has given her, but the individuals of What If If Only are insubstantial shadows.

After intermission, we get the main course, the hour-long Imp, a complex and fascinating study of wish fulfillment. We are in a seedy living room which seems to float in space (kudos to set designer Miriam Buether). Retired cousins Jimmy and Dot (Conlee and O’Connell) share the house and are entertaining their younger relative Niamh (Adelind Horan) who has moved to London from Ireland. The older cousins don’t have much going on in their lives. Jimmy has taken up jogging to relieve his depression while Dot suffers from debilitating back problems and was dismissed from her nursing job for abusing a patient. They pin their emotional needs on Niamh (pronounced Neve) who expresses irrational fear of becoming a Muslim or throwing herself under a train. 

All three become attached to Rob (Japhet Balaban), an unemployed, homeless young man, separated from his partner and their school-age son. A supernatural element is introduced when Jimmy reveals Dot has been keeping a bottle which she believes contains a magical, invisible imp.… and perhaps Jimmy believes in it, too. The influence of the imaginary (?) demon on the relationships among these four form the meat of this fourth piece. Dot treats the unseen creature like the imaginary son in Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf? She acknowledges the madness of her belief in its reality, but needs it as a means of giving color to her drab existence. Rob and Niamh are beset with fears and uncertainty while Jimmy relays sob stories from acquittances to make himself feel better by comparison. Interestingly, all of Jimmy’s stories resemble classical tragedies from the Greeks or Shakespeare, reinforcing Kill’s theme of myths, legends and literature explaining our meaningless lives. 

The cast here deliver exemplary performances of quietly desperate people yearning for purpose, but O’Connell goes a step beyond, endowing each line and gesture with the subtext of a lifetime’s disappointment. When it seems the imp has been taken from Dot, her rage threatens to destroy the theater. Hers is a devastating performance in a glass-and-convention shattering evening.

A few blocks away from the Public, Classic Stage Company is presenting a rare work by a playwright who has been as neglected as Churchill has been celebrated. Up until recently, the vibrant, thoughtful works of Alice Childress have languished. Trouble in Mind (1955) was slated for Broadway after an Off-Broadway run. But the playwright refused to make changes to its radical-for-its-time message about African-American identity in the commercial theater, and the play did not make it to the Main Stem until Roundabout Theater Company’s acclaimed 2021 revival. Now, another rarely-seen Childress work, Wine in the Wilderness is receiving a long-overdue staging at CSC, directed with passion and precision by LaChanze who starred in the Trouble revival.

Originally written for television and broadcast in 1969, Wine is set during the 1964 Harlem riots and concerns a clash between an African-American artist and the no-nonsense street survivor modeling for him. Bill Jameson needs a “beat-down chick” to pose for him to contrast to his idealized vision of African femininity. He finds Tomorrow “Tommy” Marie, who has been burned out of her home and at first fits his stereotyped idea of a crass female. But after making an honest emotional and sexual connection with Bill, Tommy finds out the true nature of the painting, and her rage matches Dot’s in the Churchill play. In a bravura acting display, Olivia Washington as Tommy defends her identity against the snobbish, unrealistic stances of Bill and his “enlightened” friends writer Sonny-man and his wife Cynthia, a social worker. Grantham Coleman captures Bill’s arrogance and final acceptance of Tommy’s complexity. Milton Craig Nealy is moving as Old-Timer, scratching out his share of dignity and Brooks Mantly and Lakisha May offer strong support as Sonny and Cynthia. 

Some of the dialogue and sexist attitudes are dated, but much more of Childress’ fiery play is totally still relevant to today’s racial conflicts. Arnulfo Maldonado’s set contains decades of African-American history and Dede Ayite’s costumes capture the contrasting social status and aspersions of the characters. This is a finely aged Wine, ready for uncorking and more pouring in future productions.

Glass. Kill. What If If Only. Imp. ****
Public Theater, 425 Lafayette St., NYC.
Running time: two hours and 15 mins. including intermission. publictheater.org
April 16 – May 11, 2025
Photography: Joan Marcus

By Samuel L. Leiter

April 18, 2025. Twelve years ago, there was a TV series called “Smash,” whose showrunner was playwright Theresa Rebeck. It was largely a backstage look at the creation of a Broadway musical called Bombshell, about the life of movie star Marilyn Monroe. Scenes from the musical, with songs by Scott Wittman and Marc Shaiman (to which songs by others were added in season two), were an important part of the series, whose title suggested a smash hit. 

Behind the scenes, the series, which began strongly, was rife with creative discord, and, when ratings fell, it ended after two seasons. Even then, the idea of eventually making the show within the series into a Broadway musical was considered. Now, after years of development, that show, also called Smash, is here, directed by Broadway A-lister Susan Stroman (The Producers), its huge list of producers led by Robert Greenblatt, Neil Meron, and Steven Spielberg, all executive producers of the TV show. The result is more of a splat than a smash. 

Many in the audience, which laughed and clapped with consistent enthusiasm, might not agree, and there are not a few critics whose thumbs were vertical, but I kept squirming under its barrage of banal dialogue, impossible characters, overwrought situations, inflated acting, and humor that seems to think that if you speak quickly at top volume, dropping a knowing look here and there, you’ll kickstart the audience into laughing.

The essential premise of the TV show—the mind-blowing tsuris that goes into the making of a Broadway musical—remains, but the dramatic, realistic qualities have been overwhelmed by farce and exaggeration. There are numerous plot and character changes, including familiar persons dropped, new ones added, and old ones revised. An obvious example is making the handsome, womanizing, British-accented director, Derek, into a pot-bellied gay man, Nigel, so he can be played with unsubtle campiness by the talented but stereotypical Brooks Ashmanskas (Once Upon a Mattress).

Where the TV show suggested a rivalry for the Marilyn role between Megan Hilty’s Ivy (here played by the terrific Robyn Hurder) and Kathryn McPhee’s Karen (now taken by a fine Carolyn Bowman, Sunset Boulevard), the musical adds a third rival, assistant director Chloe (Bella Coppola, Six), who happens to be a terrific singer, into the mix, although she’s a bit reluctant. The circumstances require Marine-like discipline to marshal your disbelief. 

Chloe, by the way, is physically unlike what you’d conventionally expect anyone playing Monroe to look like. This, uncomfortably, inspires a speech by African American producer and former actress, Anita (Jacquelyn B. Arnold, Moulin Rouge)—changed from Angelica Huston’s Eileen in the series—to give a woke speech (cue the applause) comparing her own casting difficulties getting a seat at the table to those of otherwise gifted actors who don’t “look the part,” regardless of the roles they play (like Monroe). GIVE ME A BREAK!

In one of the few bright spots, Ivy, converted here into a certified Broadway star from the series’ up and comer, gets a dynamite performance by the gorgeous, multitalented Hurder, who looks close enough in wig, costume, and makeup to MM for this fan’s approval. Her role is so ridiculously mangled, though, by writers Bob Martin (Boop! The Musical) and Rick Elice (Water for Elephants), that she becomes practically psychopathic. 

Seen at first as a warm, collaborative star, she falls under the influence of a book about Method acting given her by lyricist/book writer Tracy (Krysta Rodriguez, Into the Woods). Ivy hires the author, the bizarre, crone-like Susan Proctor (Kristine Nielsen, Vanya and Sonia and Masha and Spike,far too over the top), to be her ridiculously hovering acting coach, a reminder of the unhealthy relationship Monroe had with her own coach, Paula Strasberg. Ivy’s performance—requiring coaching on each spoken line—and behavior now becomes increasingly erratic and self-centered, especially when Susan insists she remain in character offstage, even being called Marilyn. 

This incites a psychological crisis as Ivy struggles to determine her true identity. Eventually, of course, with the show looking doomed, she learns her lesson and reforms. The whole setup is so preposterous and painfully unfunny, that it takes no time before you see not only Bombshell but Smash turning quickly into ash.

Under Stroman’s whiplash direction, Smash moves like an express train, the actors acting as if not only Monroe but everyone is on Benzedrine. Moments when things are not frenetic are few and far between. Joshua Bergasse’s choreography is pumped up and entertaining, but makes no breakthroughs; Beowulf Boritt’s multiple sets, from rehearsal rooms to a Sardi’s-like restaurant and so on, are attractive and shift smoothly; Ken Billington’s lighting delights; and Alejo Vietti’s costumes satisfy all the requirements, especially the stunning ones adorning Hurder’s curves. 

One of the few songs that appealed to me is a gentle ditty sung as it’s being composed by Tracy and her composer husband, the alcoholic Jerry (John Behlman, Shucked), “Second Hand White Baby Grand,” one of several songs that do nothing to advance the plot. And there’s also “Let’s Be Bad,” which already appeared on Broadway in the recent Some Like It Hot musical. But, these apart, the Shaiman/Wittman score is an unexciting rehash of standard Broadway music. 

Seeing Smash sosoon after Boop! The Musical—tied together by Bob Martin’s writing—brings out how close they are in their clumsy reverence for a sexy female movie star’s difficulty with identity issues, even though one’s a cartoon and the other cartoon-like. That connection is even closer when you recall Monroe singing the classic “Boop-Boop-a-Doop” song, “I Want to Be Loved by You,” in Some Like It Hot. Jasmine Amy Rogers as Betty Boop and Robyn Hurder as Marilyn Monroe are lighting up Broadway stages with screen-worthy talent, but while each is driving a wobbly vehicle Smash is the one that ends up in a crash.

Smash **
Imperial Theater, 249 W. 45th St., NYC.
Running time: two hours and 30 mins. including intermission. telecharge.com
Opened April 10, 2025. Open Run

content.rendered:
By David Sheward

April 17, 2025. During its two-season run on NBC (2012-13), I used to hate-watch Smash, the weekly series chronicling the making of a Broadway musical on screen legend Marilyn Monroe. While the musical numbers by Marc Shaiman and Scott Witman were often witty and tuneful, the melodramatic storyline was ridiculous and inaccurate in its depiction of the inner workings of show business. I always thought there was a kernel of a possibility of an exciting real Broadway show amidst the soapy excesses. Well, more than a decade later, the stage version of Smash has lived up to its name and banished all remnants of the TV show’s silly scripts.

Book-writers Bob Martin and Rick Elice have washed away the sudsy, convoluted plots from the series and incorporated many of the sleek and fun musical numbers into a tighter, funnier libretto celebrating the joys and angst of putting on a musical. The only element that remains the same is the troubled backstage brouhaha while the Monroe musical undergoes rehearsals, previews, and opening night. Many of the character names are the same, but now their characteristics are totally different. Gone are the intricate on-again, off-again romances and the focus is much tighter, all staged with economy and efficiency by Susan Stroman. Choreographer Joshua Bergasse, who also staged the dances for TV, delivers peppy, exciting ensemble work.

The main engine of the plot is now the conflict between star Ivy Lynn (a magnificent Robyn Hurder who switches admirably between devilish diva and delightful star) and the rest of the company when she commits the cardinal actor’s sin—reading a book. The tome in question is a history of Marilyn’s work with the Actors’ Studio which inspires Ivy to hire the author Susan Proctor (hilariously severe Kristine Nielsen) as an acting coach. The fanatical Susan encourages Ivy to “become” Marilyn 24/7 and replicate her impossible, pill-popping behavior off-stage. Ivy’s transformation from collaborative professional to temperamental monster is beautifully and effectively relayed in “The 20th Century Fox Mambo,” brilliantly staged by Stroman and Bergasse, interweaving Monroe’s objectification by the studio with Ivy’s descent into madness. This triggers chaos and provides an opportunity for understudy Karen (dynamic Caroline Bowman) to grab the spotlight. But wait, there’s more. Associate director Chloe (surprisingly super Bella Coppola) is also in the mix to take over the Marilyn role.

There’s also warfare between the husband-and-wife authors of the show (sharp John Behlmann and Krysta Rodriguez, the only holdover from the TV show, but winning in an entirely different role), veteran director-choreographer Nigel (a brilliantly exasperated and funny Brooks Ashmanskas), the force-of-nature producer Anita (strong and elegant Jacqueline B. Arnold), and her annoyingly naive, but ultimately life-saving, tech-savvy assistant Scott (adorable Nicholas Matos). 

This sounds as goofy as the TV show, but Martin, Elice, Shaiman, Wittman, Stroman and Bergasse manage to make it work, demonstrating the powers of collaboration their onstage counterparts lack.  

Beowulf Boritt’s clever sets, Alejo Vietti’s gorgeous costumes, and Ken Billington’s veraatile lighting create a vibrant candy-box version of Broadway.

You don’t have to be a theater nerd to enjoy Smash, but it does help. This is probably the only show with references to Mandy Patinkin in The Knife, Julie Andrews on Tik Tiok, and just about every movie Monroe ever made. But if you don’t get these allusions, it’s okay. There are plenty of laughs, songs and dance to enthrall the casual musical fan.  Smash is a smashing celebration of the joy of theater.
