By Samuel L. Leiter

April 15, 2025: Cartoon characters, like L’il Abner and Superman, have inspired several Broadway musicals, so it’s not unusual that Boop!: the Musical takes its cue from the old black and white Max Fleischer animated shorts that produced some 90 films between 1930 and 1939. Although one might think Betty Boop something of a niche character, this adorably sexy, miniskirted, big-eyed, bobbed-hair, spit-curled flapper—with one visible garter—remains familiar enough to make her the titular heart of this expensively glitzy new Broadway show at the Broadhurst Theatre.

The idea of a Betty Boop musical—this one has been in development for years and had a good run in Chicago—could have gone in several ways, one being to stay in period, another to move it forward. Book writer Bob Martin (Elf, Smash) tries to do both, his script beginning as a faux black and white 1930s movie cartoon (artfully executed), which goes behind the scenes to introduce not only Betty (Jasmine Amy Rogers, terrific casting) and her Grampy (Stephen DeRosa), but her jodhpur-wearing, megaphone-carrying director Oscar Delacorte (Aubie Merryless), and his knickered assistant director, Clarence (Ricky Schroeder).

Being cartoon characters in a cartoon world, they’re allowed free rein to behave as cartoonishly as they wish, which only makes them—Betty aside—increasingly unbearable. Something’s got to be off when—again, Betty aside—the most believable character is Grampy’s dog, Pudgy, a tiny, white, string puppet. nicely handled in full view by Phillip Huber.

The groan-worthy premise, carried out with umpteen stock tropes, is that Grampy, an eccentric, Rube Goldberg-ish inventor (think Doc Brown in Back to the Future), has created a huge, armchair-like, time traveling machine that projects Betty into present-day New York (think Elf)where she lands, naturally, at a Comic-Con convention, surrounded by cosplay comics characters; of course, being one herself, she fits right in. Our job is to accept that this pen and ink figure is now a full-fleshed human being—she soon trades her black and white threads for more colorful ones—able to befriend and, indeed, fall in love with real people.

Through her newfound friends, Dwayne (Ainsley Melham), a handsome trumpeter at a jazz club; Trisha (Angelica Hale), an artsy, Betty Boop-obsessed teenaged orphan; and Trisha’s politically active aunt, Carol Evans (Anastacia McCleskey), Betty becomes enmeshed in the campaign of Raymond Demarest (Erich Bergen), a slimy egotist running for New York’s mayor. His campaign brands him as the “doo doo” mayor, which is about as funny as things get. Oh, and Grampy goes back to the future as well, even rekindling an affair with old flame Valentina (Faith Prince), an astrophysicist. I’m still trying to figure that one out.

This is the kind of show that used to be excused on the grounds that it would appeal to the tired businessman. You’d have to be very tired indeed to appreciate the silliness displayed, especially since so much of the humor is as flatly two-dimensional as a Betty Boop cartoon.

Nor is David Foster’s generic music—mixing jazz and standard Broadway styles—anything to enthuse about at the office water cooler. Understandably, no attempt is made in the staging to reflect the special quality of the shorts, in which physical objects—even mustaches—are as animate as living creatures. Less understandably, the distinct, 1930s musical manner of the shorts is also totally ignored.

There are themes, of course, like the familiar one about the need to find and be true to oneself, embodied in Betty’s journey from a time when she was confused about her multifaceted identity (as per her opening song, “A Little Versatility”). But these are as cliched as almost everything else, including an 11 o’clock power ballad, “Something to Shout About,” which practically shouts that “this is the 11 o’clock power ballad!”

The two-act show, however, which runs two and a half hours, with one intermission, is not without its bonbons, especially in the second act, the better of the two. I especially enjoyed a number in which the would-be mayor chases Betty around a desk, spoofing what Betty hated about her movie roles. Erich Bergen’s slickly handsome, pompously self-assured, would-be Lothario packs enough comic punch and character-delineating shtick to forgive many of the show’s less memorable moments.

There’s also a sprightly comic duet, “Whatever It Takes,” for the old lovers, Grampy and Valentina, that gives the otherwise underused Prince something to smile about. It would be better if Foster’s insufficiently earwormy tune were more worthy of distinguished veteran Susan Birkenhead’s brightly charming lyrics.

Jasmine Amy Rogers, making a splashy Broadway debut, has been cunningly wigged (by Sabana Majeed), made up, and costumed to resemble Betty. Gifted with an incandescent smile, she does all the right things, singing, dancing, and acting her heart out to give her flimsy role a semblance of three-dimensional life. But don’t expect that squeaky “Boop-Opp-A-Doops” voice from the cartoons; Rogers is every bit the belter that a Broadway show requires. Ainsley Melham, infusing another cardboard role with a semblance of a heartbeat, displays solid song and dance chops. Everyone else is as satisfactory as such material warrants, and the glittery visuals, sets by David Rockwell, lights by Philip S. Rosenberg, projections by Finn Ross, and, especially, costumes by Gregg Barnes are everything you’d expect of a well-produced Broadway musical comedy.

Barnes not only reproduces just what Betty should look like, he designs one particularly clever number, “Where is Betty?” so that the chorus wears costumes with one side black and white, the reverse in Technicolor. Director-choreographer Jerry Mitchell does his magic whenever the dancers turn around.

Boop!: the Musical, while occasionally amusingly cute, colorfully energetic, and sentimentally heartwarming, is more often just silly and dull. Remember when Marilyn Monroe sang “I Want to Be Loved by You” in Some Like It Hot? “Boop-Oop-A-Doops” has never been the same.

Boop!: The Musical

By Samuel L. Leiter

April 14, 2025: The current Broadway season, which technically ends this month, has been notably top-heavy with musicals and pencil thin in new plays. However, for those pondering the upcoming awards deliberations, the last few weeks have seen several potent arrivals in the latter category. I’m talking about Purpose, The Picture of Dorian Gray, Good Night, and Good Luck, and, now, John Proctor Is the Villian, at the Booth Theatre. This latter, by Atlanta playwright Kimberly Belflower, makes a decent case for why it should be a contender. Occasional faults aside, its subject matter will hopefully attract a younger audience (if they can afford it!).

John Proctor Is the Villain is built around another play, although not in the same way as Tom Stoppard’s Rosencrantz and Guildenstern is built around Hamlet. Here the inspiration is Arthur Miller’s The Crucible, still an important part of many school curricula, although it’s been banned by certain institutions. My granddaughter, a Long Island high school English teacher, informs me that her school removed it at the behest of the Jehovah’s Witnesses.

It continues, however, to get numerous amateur and professional productions; because of its position among liberal academicians, it’s a college theatre warhorse. I directed many college plays, but none packed them in like The Crucible. I suspect there’s a large academic market out there for Belflowers’s play, at least those that won’t, like the teacher in this play, keep reprimanding it for “Language!”

Premiered at Washington, D.C.’s, Studio Theatre in 2022, presented at Boston’s Huntington Theatre in 2024, and seen in several university productions, John Proctor Is the Villain’s intermissionless hour and 45 minutes all take place in a single classroom, realistically designed by AMP, featuring Teresa Williams, and effectively lit (strobe lights and all) by Natasha Katz. Situated in a rural, one-stoplight (soon there’ll be two), Christian town in north Georgia, the play focuses on a small AP English class of seven juniors (five girls and two boys). Also present are two others: the hip, smart, attentive, and attractive teacher, Mr. Carter Smith (Gabriel Ebert), and a pretty, well-meaning counselor, Miss Bailey Gallagher (Molly Griggs). Both are graduates of the school, although she’s somewhat younger.

The play’s rural locale may conjure memories of Deliverance, but there’s nothing backwoods about the quality of the education, nor—the slacker boys aside—the intelligence of its most ambitious, if sex-obsessed students. In fact, take away the profane, “like”-filled, teenage slang and immature syntax, not to mention Mr. Smith’s full-throated support of each student’s feedback, and you can imagine being in a college freshman class; on the other hand, the girls sometimes seem a bit too advanced for classroom authenticity. This is, after all, a message play, and the didacticism is never far away.

The time is 2018, smack dab in the #MeToo movement. The girls, led by the aggressively ambitious, overachieving Beth (Fina Strazza), who tosses around terms like “intersectional feminism,” start an extracurricular club to examine feminist issues. It works as a wall off which to bounce the play’s concerns.

These, as spotlit by the title, imagine that the “hot” Mr. Smith’s class—where sex education is also on the syllabus, and abstinence is promoted—is studying Arthur Miller’s 1953 The Crucible (sections of which are recited, with the approval of the playwright’s estate). Circumstances surrounding the relationship between the married Mr. Smith and a student, Shelby Holcomb (Sadie Sink), reflect those of Miller’s character, John Proctor, a married man, and young Abigail Williams, the girl with whom he had sex and whom he rejects as a “whore.”

The bright but raging Shelby has been sent to Atlanta for several months for reasons that gradually emerge; when she returns and takes part in The Crucible discussions, she proposes that Proctor—widely deemed an example of moral heroism—is really a villain.

It will be remembered that The Crucible, set in the late 1690s, reenacts the Salem, Massachusetts, witch trials, and that Proctor, deeming it necessary to protect his name, goes to his death rather than falsely confess to witchcraft.It had other purposes than those of Belflower’s play, principally being to serve as an allegory for those confronted by the congressional anticommunist hearings of the day, a subject even now being examined nearby in the George Clooney starrer, Good Night, and Good Luck. For all its good intentions, John Proctor Is the Villian skips any suggestion that the #MeToo movement may have fostered its own witch hunt frenzy.

Shelby’s response to Proctor’s defense of his “name” in contrast to the lived experience of Abigail’s body is one of Belflower’s highlights, contrasting the man’s rhetorical trope against the woman’s physical fact. When it comes to Shelby’s game-changing declaration, which I won’t describe, it’s certainly a shocker, but its motivations for being expressed at this juncture remain cloudy, and only heighten her unpleasantness. Perhaps it’s her newfound exposure to The Crucible, in which she says no one listened to Abigail’s accusations, adding that people now must listen to those like her.  

We’re in a high school environment, so sex is on everyone’s mind, reflected even in the pop music references, which include Taylor Swift and her reportedly noxious relationship with John Mayer (you learn something every day), and Lorde, whose “Green Light” plays an important, even exorcistic, role in the dramedy. (Warning: older viewers, like me, may need to Google some of the pop culture references.) Soon, we begin, justified or not. to suspect each interchange between a male and female to have hidden innuendoes, and sometimes between the females themselves.

The episodic script, linked by Palmer Heffernan’s spot-on interstitial music, reveals sexual tensions among the students, of course, as in a scene where a boy named Lee (Hagan Oliveras) expresses his frustration with his girlfriend of seven years, Raelynne (Amalia Yoo), by a minor act of violence. Male toxicity is never far from the surface. Even one of the girls’ fathers, accused of improper dalliance—he claims he’s the victim of a witch hunt—gets tossed in the grinder, making all men suspect or, like the other male student, Mason (Nihar Duvvuri), clueless.

Under Danya Taymor’s fast-paced, nicely articulated staging, the cast, whose high schoolers, as usual, are played by slightly older actors, is funny and energetic, with uniformly quality performances. Sadie Sink has the most into which to sink her teeth, and brings a good balance of anger and sensitivity to Shelby. Gabriel Ebert, a familiar Broadway presence, is always engaging; even with his “y’all” Georgia drawl, he’s consistently sympathetic, regardless of what his Mr. Smith may or may not have done.

John Proctor Is the Villain is part feminist tract, part hormonal high school dramedy, and part literature lesson. Most audiences should find something here to satisfy their cravings.

John Proctor is the Villian ****
Booth Theatre, 222 W. 45th Street NYC.
Running time: 1oo mins. no intermission. johnproctoristhevillain.com
Open run.

By Paulanne Simmons

April 15, 2025. From the moment the dancers, dressed in sparkling tuxes, prance onto the stage at the Broadhurst Theatre and perform a number that includes an incredible tap and a rotating kick line, we know Boop! The Musical, with director and choreographer Jerry Mitchell at the helm, is going to be one hell of a good time.

The musical, with a book by Bob Martin, music by David Foster and lyrics by Susan Birkenhead, captures all the energy of the animated cartoon character, Betty Boop, designed by Grim Natwick for the films produced by Max Fleischer between 1930 and 1939. Betty Boop was a Jazz Age flapper and a symbol of the Depression era. She had a big round face with large eyes, a tiny red mouth and a button nose framed by tight black curls. She wore short skirts with a garter on her thigh. Unlike other female cartoon characters, Betty Boop was sexy, and as a result, was often the prey of predatory men.

The fabulous Jasmine Amy Rogers, in her Broadway debut as Betty, is all this, and much more. We first see Betty in her black-and-white comic world. But she is tired of her celebrity, and, with the help of the time-travel machine created by Grampy (Stephen DeRosa), makes it to the very colorful New York City.

At first, Betty is timid and unsure, but at a Javitz Center Comic Con she encounters the aspiring musician Dwayne (Ainsley Melham) and his adorable, orphaned cousin, Trisha (the formidable Angelica Hale), a budding artist. Soon Betty meets Trisha’s guardian, Carol (Anastacia McCleskey), who is singlehandedly running the campaign of the secretly corrupt mayoral candidate, Raymond Demarest (Erich Bergen, worth all the money his character is trying to steal). It isn’t until Dwayne, who is quickly falling in love with Betty, asks her to sing at his favorite jazz club, and Demarest asks Betty to use her celebrity to boost his campaign that Betty comes into her own, learns to become who she really wants to be and teaches that lesson to her new friends.

In the meantime, Grampy, desperate to get Betty to come home, follows her to New York City, bringing with him Pudgy, Betty’s pug, a marionette whose legs, tail and lovingly licking tongue are operated by the puppeteer Phillip Huber. But while Grampy is trying to find Betty, he meets Valentina (the always winning Faith Prince), an astrophysicist he had fallen in love with 40 years ago on his last trip to the real world. Their song-and-dance number, “Whatever It Takes,” is one of the musical’s most delightful.

Boop is an expansive, old-fashioned musical. The score is big and brassy. The singers belt out the upbeat songs and linger lovingly on the ballads. Costume designer Gregg Barnes has created extravagant costumes in black-and-white and full color. “Where Is Betty,” which opens Act 2, features costumes that are black-and-white on one side and full color on the other, adding visual glee to the dancing. And David Rockwell’s sets make the black-and-white world, and the real world seem equally fantastical in their own way.

Some people may take great pleasure looking down their nose at the sheer silliness of Boop! That’s their right. But most people will have a better time just joining in the merriment.

BOOP! The Musical ****
Broadhurst Theater, 235 W. 44th St., NYC.

By David Sheward

April 13, 2025. The Broadway premiere of The Last Five Years at the Hudson,Jason Robert Brown’s two-character tuner chronicling the romance, marriage and break-up of novelist Jamie and actress Cathy, is a mixed affair. (The intimate musical debuted Off-Broadway in 2002, was revived by Second Stage in 2013, and was made into a movie in 2014.) Boy-band heartthrob Nick Jonas gives an uneven performance, his co-star Adrienne Warren is on point throughout, and director Whitney White’s staging is mostly smooth but at times muddies the show’s central conceit. 

Brown’s clever structure underlines the central theme of missed connections. The show is mostly sung-through with each character expressing their emotions in alternating solos. Cathy starts by reading Jamie’s break-up letter and moves backwards in time while Jamie opens with his excitement at their first meeting and proceeds forwards over the half-decade of their union. In the original, the only time they appear onstage together is in the middle when they marry. For this production, the leads silently appear in each other’s scenes. Whether this was White’s or Brown’s decision, it confuses the dual timeline and lessens the impact of their one duet, the only moment in the show when their affections overlap. Otherwise, White’s direction flows freely from song to song with the aide of David Zinn’s suggestive, mobile sets and Stacey Derosier’s mood-focusing lighting.

The stars are both talented, capable performers, but Warren consistently conveys the varying emotions beneath her songs while Jonas doesn’t come up to full subtextual strength until half-way through the score. There’s no excuse for Jonas’ half-baked performance. He’s not just some lightweight pop teen idol. He’s been on Broadway since he was a child, appearing in Annie Get Your Gun, Beauty and the Beast and Les Miserables, as well as replacing Daniel Radcliffe in the 2011 How to Succeed revival. So he should know what he’s doing.

 

The trouble starts with Jamie’s first number “Shiksa Goddess,” a funny litany of the Jewish girls he has dated before finding the Gentile Cathy. Jonas has no comic timing here and misses all the laughs. The same with his next song, “Moving Too Fast” where he seems more interested in hitting and holding high notes than in conveying Jamie’s anxiety over success in his work and love life coming too quickly. Stacey Derosier has provided a bank of light bulbs on the back wall which do the emotional work Jonas fails to enact by popping on and off at appropriate moments.

Jonas finally finds his feet after the shared honeymoon scene with “A Miracle Would Happen” in which Jamie comically reveals his frustration that now that he’s married, women find him attractive. He hits the gags and finds the humor in Jamie’s ironic situation rather than just sustaining notes. (By the way, I found it hard to believe Jonas as the somewhat nerdy Jamie. Donning a pair of glasses and carrying a tote bag from the Strand Bookstore failed to convincingly transform the sexy heartthrob into a serious, unsure-of-himself author.) From this midway point, Jonas captures Jamie’s rising unhappiness with his marriage and his ambivalence towards Cathy, still loving her, but unable to tolerate her insecurities. 

Meanwhile, Warren, a Tony winner for dynamically playing Tina Turner, fully exposes Cathy’s conflicting feelings in every one of her songs. In her opening “Still Hurting” she is a walking raw wound. In “See I’m Smiling,” we see her joy at Jamie joining her during a summer stock gig in Ohio, and then she gradually peels back the surface layers of cheerfulness to reveal her anger when he leaves early to attend a literary function. She’s funny in “A Summer in Ohio,” listing the drawbacks of small-time stage work and her bizarre castmates including a snake named Wayne, and heartbreaking during a riotous audition sequence civilizing her scrambled inner thoughts while trying out for a musical. White gives her clever business during these two numbers, such as having her pull props out of a bottomless trunk in the former and including an onstage accompanist for Warren to react to in the latter. 

Tom Murray’s musical direction effectively delivers Brown’s multiple styles and Dede Ayite designed the beautiful costumes (I especially enjoyed Cathy’s gorgeous wedding dress.) 

For The Last Five Years to succeed, both players must deliver equally vibrant turns. Here we only get one and half, so it’s more like a strong three years and six months. 

The Last Five Years ***

Running time: 90 minutes, no intermission. thelastfiveyearsbroadway.com

A delightful musical homage to the iconic cartoon character directed by veteran Jerry Mitchell.

By Patrick Christiano

April 11, 2025: Boop! The Musical is a delightful homage to the iconic cartoon character created by Max Fleischer in the 1930s and embodied beautifully by Jasmine Amy Rogers making her Broadway debut as Betty Boop, a role she originated in the pre-Broadway Chicago run.  Director and choreographer, Jerry Mitchell, brings his trademark flair with a bright and breezy production, a colorful pastiche, which kept me smiling throughout the evening.

Bored with her celebrity life making short black and white films, one after another, Betty embarks on an interdimensional journey with the help her Grampy, a lively Stephen DeRosa, who has invented a chair, a “trans-dimensional tempus locus actuating electro-ambulator” which transports Betty right into the middle of modern-day Comic Con in New York City 2025.

Up until this point the whole production was in black and white, the creation of set designer David Rockwell, with costumes by Gregg Barnes and lighting by Philip S. Rosenberg. Suddenly the stage surges into a kaleidoscope of color and the background dancers are costumed in bright vibrant sparkling colors. The transformation is stunning and kicks the production into another gear.

At Comic Con Betty meets an adorable jazz musician, Dwayne, played by Ainsley Melham, who will become her love interest. She also meets Trisha, a spunky Angelica Hale, who is a longtime fan of Betty’s.  Dwayne keeps an eye on Trisha for her aunt Carol, played by Anastacia McCleskey, and quickly takes an interest in Betty. And Betty in turn, new to the world of color, is fascinated by Dwayne’s blue eyes.

Soom Betty, a symbol of charm for a century, will find herself in the middle of politics because Carol is working for Raymond Demarest, a candidate for mayor, who is behind in the polls, played by an amusing Erich Bergen. He enlists Betty’s assistance for public appearances and begins to soar in the polls, creating a dilemma for Betty. However, she will rise to the occasion while discovering a deeper understanding of who she is and her effect on others.

The story, a slight, simplistic tale about knowing your own worth is brought to life by a spirited cast of outstanding performers guided by a two-time Tony award winning choreographer. The clever book by Bob Martin, who co-wrote The Drowsy Chaperone, displays a fondness for the characters. The high- spirited toe-tapping music is by the 16- time grammy winning composer, David Foster, with lyrics by Susan Birkenhead.

There is a tangent tale, which involves Grampy and his old fame, Valentina, played by a wonderfully funny Faith Prince, about the two reviving their relationship after losing contact for years.

Betty is the quintessential cartoon jazz baby inspired by singer Helen Kane famous for her “boop-opp-a-doop” tag line to songs like “I Wanna Be Loved by You.” Her distinctive mini-skirted look is instantly recognizable, a big head, spit- curled dark hair, large round eyes, and a pouty mouth. Jasmine Amy Rogers is the perfect incarnation with the prerequisite Betty Boop curves and look, she radiates charm the moment she makes her entrance, and you are taken back by the uncanny resemblance.  She is a triple threat, singer, dancer, actress, and her confident performance is a joy to witness.

Boop is an old-fashioned feel -good musical, the perfect antidote for our troubled times.

BOOP! The Musical ****

Running time: two hours and 20 mins. including intermission. www.boopthemusical.com
